Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_associated_pow: The equality v(π) = 1 implies π is nonzero and v(πⁿ) = n. Since v(x) = n as well, the ratio x/πⁿ has valuation zero. It belongs to the valuation ring and is a unit there. Multiplying πⁿ by this unit gives x, proving that the elements are associated.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_exists_nat: By discreteness the valuation of the nonzero element x is finite, so it is represented by an integer m. Membership in the valuation ring gives m ≥ 0. Take the natural number represented by m.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_irreducible: An element of valuation 1 is not a unit, since units have valuation zero. If π = ab, the two factors have nonnegative valuations whose sum is 1. Neither valuation can be the top element, and the remaining values are nonnegative integers. One of the two values is therefore zero. The corresponding factor is a unit, proving irreducibility.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_isDiscreteValuationRing: Choose π of valuation 1 using normalized discreteness. It lies in the valuation ring and is irreducible. Every nonzero element has a finite nonnegative integer valuation n and is associated to πⁿ. The criterion that a ring with such a uniformizer and factorization is a discrete valuation ring now applies.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_isUnit_iff:
If x has an inverse y in the valuation ring, the valuations of x and y are nonnegative and sum to the valuation of 1, which is zero. Thus v(x) = 0.

Conversely, v(x) = 0 implies x ≠ 0 because the valuation of zero is the top element. The inverse has valuation −0 = 0 and belongs to the valuation ring. Together with the inverse identity in the field, this makes x a unit in the valuation ring.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_map_inv: The valuation of an inverse is the negative of the valuation of the original element. Applying this identity and substituting v(x) = n gives v(x⁻¹) = −n.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.normDiscrete_mem_vRing_iff: By definition, the valuation ring consists of the elements with nonnegative valuation. Applying this definition to x gives the equivalence.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.finsum_fiberwise_of_finite_support:
Let S be the finite support of f. For each b, the sum of f on the fibre ρ⁻¹(b) is the finite sum over those a in S with ρ(a) = b. To see this, extend the summand on the fibre by zero to all of A. The extension is supported in S, and the terms outside the fibre vanish.

If b lies outside ρ(S), the fibre sum is zero. The outer sum can therefore be taken over the finite image ρ(S). The fibres over this image partition S, so adding their sums gives the sum of f over S, which is the original finitely supported sum.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.localization_away_injective_of_dvd:
Let I be the kernel of R → R_𝔭 and choose a finite generating set for I using Noetherianity. Each generator maps to zero in R_𝔭, so some element outside 𝔭 annihilates it. Take t to be the product of these elements, using 1 for the empty set. The complement of 𝔭 is multiplicatively closed, so t is outside 𝔭. It annihilates each generator and therefore all of I.

Write c = td and fix a compatible map κ from R[1/c] to R_𝔭. The images of t and d multiply to the unit image of c, so the image of t is a unit in R[1/c]. If a fraction a/cⁿ belongs to the kernel of κ, multiplying its image by the image of cⁿ shows that a maps to zero in R_𝔭. Hence a lies in I and ta = 0. Since t maps to a unit in R[1/c], a maps to zero there as well. The fraction is zero and κ is injective.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.X_pow_mul_C_mem_coneAlg: Let W be the range of ev. Induct on the construction of t as an element of Wᵈ. In degree zero, a ground scalar gives a constant polynomial, which lies in the algebra. Addition of elements of Wᵈ corresponds to addition of their degree-d monomials. In the multiplication step write the new coefficient as ev(v)t′, with t′ in the preceding power. Its monomial is the product of X·C(ev(v)) and the monomial for t′. The first factor is a generator of the cone algebra and the second belongs by induction.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.mem_coneAlg_iff_coeff:
Write W for the range of ev. For the forward direction, the condition that the coefficient of degree d belongs to Wᵈ is preserved by the operations generating the algebra. The generator X·C(ev(v)) has its only possibly nonzero coefficient in degree one, where it lies in W. Ground scalars contribute only in degree zero, where W⁰ is the ground-scalar submodule. The condition is closed under addition degree by degree. In a product, each contribution to degree d is a product of coefficients from degrees i and j with i+j=d, so it belongs to WⁱWʲ = Wᵈ. The sum of these contributions also belongs.

Conversely, expand p as the finite sum of its coefficient monomials. The preceding lemma puts each monomial Xᵈ·C(p_d) in the algebra because p_d belongs to Wᵈ. Closure under finite addition gives p in the cone algebra.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.coercive_of_re_pos:
Write q(x) = Re Q(x,x). If V has only the zero vector, q(0) = 0 by bilinearity and c = 1 suffices. Suppose V has a nonzero vector. Linear maps from a finite-dimensional normed space are continuous, so Q can be viewed as a continuous linear map into the space of continuous linear maps V → ℂ. Evaluating on the diagonal and taking the real part gives a continuous function q.

The unit sphere is nonempty and compact, so q has a minimum c there. Every unit vector is nonzero, hence the positivity hypothesis gives c > 0. For x ≠ 0, set u = x/‖x‖. Then u has norm one, and bilinearity gives q(x) = ‖x‖² q(u) ≥ ‖x‖² c. At x = 0 both sides vanish.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.GlobalTheory.Fc.of_hyps: Apply the shape theorem to the family and selections carried by the hypothesis record. Pass the S-component of each C-selection. Translate the divisibility rows and the service condition using their equivalences in the shape interface. For the rank rows, retain the existing constants and eventual threshold, and keep the listed fields of the first row together with the second row intact. This gives the row condition in the form required by the shape theorem. The record and the supplied proofs of V and NR give all remaining inputs, so the theorem yields G.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.GlobalTheory.Fc.shape_of: Fix the four parameters and the shape theorem. Apply of_hyps with the supplied proofs of V and NR and the family hypothesis record to obtain G.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.rootOfUnity_mem_range_Om: Choose a primitive mth root ζ in Om ℓ. The embedding into ℂ_[ℓ] is injective, so the image of ζ is still primitive of order m. Its m powers from exponent 0 through m−1 are distinct roots of X^m−1. Since that polynomial has degree m, these exhaust its roots. In particular x is one of those powers. The same power of ζ in Om ℓ maps to x because the embedding preserves powers.

Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.Val.pow:
Unpack the normal-form data for a value of x. Each entry of the two characteristic vectors is either zero or one half, so both vectors coincide pointwise with their real-part vectors viewed over ℂ. The power formula for normal forms then gives the transformed data for y and its determinant relation.

Use the transformed data as the witnesses for the value of y. The new constant is cʲ and is nonzero because c is nonzero. Substituting the determinant relation and combining the powers gives the value tʲ.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.exists_known_rat:
Start with the rational elliptic curve y² = x³ − x. Its elliptic key has genus one and known value equal to the discriminant. Take its gth key power to get genus g. The proposed known value is the gth power of the discriminant.

After extension to ℂ, choose normal-form data for the original elliptic key. The discriminant formula gives its value in this normal form. The key power raises that value to the gth power by the formula for values of key powers. The base-change comparison and cancellation identify this normal form with the one for the given complex key of genus g, giving the required known value.
Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/.isElliptic_cube_sub: Compute the Weierstrass invariants of the model y² = x³ − x and substitute them in the discriminant formula. The discriminant is 64. It is nonzero, hence a unit in ℚ, which is the ellipticity criterion for the model.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.factor_ne_zero: The prime p exceeds 1, and Re(s) is positive, so the norm of p^(−s) is p^(−Re(s)) < 1. The norm of the character value is at most 1, hence the norm of their product is strictly below 1. The product cannot equal 1, which proves the Euler factor is nonzero.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.gamma_ne_zero: Distinguish even and odd characters. Their gamma factors are Γℝ(s) and Γℝ(s + 1), respectively. Positive real part of s implies positive real part of both arguments, so the factors are nonzero.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.prim_reflect: The gamma factor is nonzero at s, so the zero of the ordinary L-function gives a zero of the completed L-function. The inverse character is primitive by invariance of the conductor under inversion. Its functional equation transfers the completed zero to 1 − s. Since 1 − s is distinct from zero, the expression for the ordinary L-function in terms of the completed one gives the desired zero.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.prim_zero: The change-of-level formula expresses the original L-value as the primitive L-value times a product of Euler factors. Here s is distinct from 1 because Re(s) < 1. Each Euler factor is nonzero since Re(s) > 0 makes the term subtracted from 1 have absolute value less than 1. The product can therefore vanish only through the primitive L-value.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.strip: A zero above the critical line in real part contradicts right half-plane nonvanishing. For a zero below the critical line, first pass to the primitive character using the change-of-level formula. Its functional equation gives a zero at 1 − s for the inverse character. The reflected point has real part greater than 1/2 and is distinct from 1 because Re(s) > 0. This contradicts the same nonvanishing hypothesis, leaving Re(s) = 1/2.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.zeta:
A zero with real part at least 1 contradicts the usual zeta nonvanishing theorem. When the real part lies strictly between 0 and 1, view zeta as the L-function of the character of modulus 1 and apply the Dirichlet critical-strip result.

It remains to consider Re(s) ≤ 0. The value at zero is nonzero. The exclusions on s also ensure Γℝ(s) is nonzero, since its other zeros are the negative even integers. Thus the completed zeta function vanishes at s. Its functional equation transfers the zero to 1 − s, where the ordinary zeta function would then vanish with real part at least 1. This is impossible.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.zeta_iff: Both statements say that every zero of the zeta function other than 1 and the negative even integers has real part 1/2. Each direction follows by using the same hypothesis on those zeros.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.topDesWin:
Combine the nine closed link conditions into one. Let ε₁ be its positive cutoff and ε₃ the positive cutoff for design existence. For 0 < ε < min(ε₁, ε₃), choose the threshold K given by the combined closed condition. Design existence above K produces a family in 𝒞′, together with its chosen data and size bounds. Map its class membership to 𝒞 to apply the closed conditions and to ℰ for the conclusion.

The ℰ membership gives the eventual volume bound. Use it with the N-link and the small-level rank equality to obtain divisibility in N. The closed divisibility condition, together with the eta and size inputs, then gives the required divisibility link. Combine this with the rank conditions and the two size estimates to obtain the μ-link. The global link now applies to the G, S, irreducibility, divisibility, and μ-links, producing the tied family required for connectedness.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.plugAll: First apply the preceding theorem to obtain the zero-free statement for primitive characters. Apply the imprimitive reduction to extend that statement to every Dirichlet character.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.plugWin: Take a witness of the family hypotheses. The Green condition supplies the shape theorem for these families, and applying it to the witness gives the connectedness criterion for the required families. For each primitive character ψ, the window input at ψ gives the required host existence by the host existence theorem for a character window. Apply the primitive-character nonvanishing theorem with these two inputs and window parameter 3/2, which exceeds 1.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.hostOfField: Apply the host construction from field data. It takes the uniform short-norm estimates, including the estimate with norm bound one. With those inputs fixed, the construction supplies the constants and, for each admissible field datum in range, a host together with the required sharing estimate.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.supplyOfAdm: The general supply theorem converts admissible rank data and a character window into host existence. Use the preceding field-to-host construction. The resulting hosts satisfy both the cyclic-level estimate and the volume bound at the square root of the scale parameter.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.imprimitive:
Let ψ be the primitive character inducing χ. Primitive nonvanishing gives L(ψ,s) ≠ 0. If χ is nonprincipal, then ψ is nonprincipal, since changing the level of a principal character still gives a principal character. If s ≠ 1 this condition on the character is unnecessary. Thus the hypotheses allow the change-of-level formula for L(χ,s).

That formula multiplies L(ψ,s) by factors 1 − ψ(p)p^(−s). For each prime p in the product, |ψ(p)| ≤ 1 and |p^(−s)| = p^(−Re(s)) < 1, since p > 1 and Re(s) > 1/2. Hence ψ(p)p^(−s) cannot be 1. All factors in the formula are nonzero, so L(χ,s) is nonzero.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.FinalTheorems.everyCharacter: The integral Galois compatibility theorem applied to the local reciprocity parameter gives the compatibility hypothesis of the preceding nonvanishing result. That result applies to every character.

Use the Galois compatibility hypothesis to supply both compatibility entries of the literature hypotheses. The local reciprocity existence theorem supplies the remaining entry. The same Galois compatibility hypothesis gives the required window estimate. Apply the nonvanishing theorem with these literature hypotheses and that estimate.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.FinalTheorems.riemannHypothe: The preceding theorem supplies nonvanishing to the right of the critical line for all Dirichlet characters. The reduction from this nonvanishing statement gives the Riemann Hypothesis.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.riemannHypothesis_of_everyCh:
Let s be a nontrivial zero of the zeta function, with s ≠ 1. The right half-plane nonvanishing just proved rules out Re(s) > 1/2. Suppose Re(s) < 1/2. The value ζ(0) = −1/2 gives s ≠ 0. Then 1 − s is distinct from both 0 and 1, and Re(1 − s) > 1/2.

Write ζ(s) as the completed zeta function divided by Γℝ(s). A zero of Γℝ occurs only at 0 or a negative even integer, and both possibilities are excluded here. Hence the completed zeta function vanishes at s. Its functional equation gives the same zero at 1 − s. The quotient formula there gives ζ(1 − s) = 0, contradicting right half-plane nonvanishing. Thus Re(s) = 1/2.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.zeta_ne_zero_of_everyCharact: Take the unique character modulo 1. Its L-function is the Riemann zeta function. Apply the assumed nonvanishing to this character and the given point s. The hypothesis s ≠ 1 supplies the required disjunction even for the principal character.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.shapeWin:
Build the closed conditions for the design theorem from the given selections. The real-place tie, mass ratio, and genus mass inputs give the chosen-rank condition and the global link by the global-link theorem. To obtain the divisibility condition, first collect the restriction rows, stable cuts, chosen rows, one-map condition, nonnegative size, admissible twist link, and the two selection conditions. These conditions hold together by closure. For a family satisfying them, the wiring selection supplies the row maps when the required N-link is available. Use these maps and the collected conditions to form the bridge rows, then use the closed divisibility-link theorem.

For the existence input, intersect the original family class with the requested G-class. Restrict the selection and duty to this intersection. Forgetting the G-condition gives the original twisted and smoothed families, so the closed size and level conditions restrict as well. The design existence theorem now supplies designs in the intersection. Apply the design-window theorem with those designs, the closed divisibility condition just proved, and the eta, irreducibility, rank, G, S, and global links. The resulting connectedness is that of the requested G-class.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.at_of_from: The From relation identifies the ranks of the point with R and identifies the transported host data with those of H. It also identifies the images of the two sets TT in the ambient frame coordinates. The frame coordinate map is injective, so equality of images gives equality of the sets themselves. After these identifications, the defining arguments of G.At at the point are exactly the arguments in the hypothesis on G.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.UpperTheory.Top.supplyChi: Fix ψ and its window input. The admissible-host supply theorem reduces the conclusion to producing an admitted rank datum for each sufficiently large scale with the specified order and character-kernel conditions. For each ε in the required range, choose the threshold from the twisted-character admissibility theorem. After identifying the scale parameter with ε, the scale, order, and host assumptions are exactly those used by that theorem. Its rank datum supplies the admissible rank data required for host existence.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.eFamC_of_cls: Use the constant 4 and the eventual threshold x₁ + 1. The character-family hypothesis supplies the cyclic-level estimate at the chosen host. Its scale coordinates are x and ε, by the two scale identities for the family. Substituting these coordinates gives the asserted eventual condition.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.hypV_of_cls: Take the eventual threshold x₁ + 1. At each x beyond this threshold and each index i, membership in the character family gives the two bounds at the corresponding host. The second is the required eventual volume bound.
Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/Charac.zeroFreeAll_of_topG: Use the cyclic tied-window nonvanishing theorem with the given scaled families and their chain relation. Its comparison hypotheses are the level bound on family scales and the form-B theorem. For each ψ, apply the connectedness criterion using the host existence and eventual volume bound for the family class of ψ. This gives the exponents, a positive ε cutoff, and the required families. Each family supplies the eventual cyclic-level estimate by the preceding lemma, its windows directly from class membership, and the tie data from connectedness. The resulting nonvanishing theorem applies to every primitive character.

Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/ThetaC.UpperTheory.LiteratureTheorems.every_cha: Obtain the eigenvalue and first-stage results from the literature interface O. The same interface yields agreement of the theta integrals and local matching. Use the geometric and arithmetic results in O, together with the Hilbert–Samuel and bigness estimates, to obtain the covolume estimate. Supply these inputs, the local reciprocity existence theorem, and the window hypothesis to the nonvanishing result based on theta-integral agreement and local matching.

Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.comparison_degree_one_bijective: A degree-one cochain is indexed by pairs of objects T, T′ and arrows T → T′. On the component for an arrow the semilinear comparison acts by the component map at T′. Its lift is bijective by the objectwise bijectivity lemma. Apply the finite-product lemma to the arrows for each fixed pair, then to T′ for each T, and finally to T.
Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.comparison_degree_two_bijective: A degree-two cochain is indexed by triples of objects T, T′, T″ and composable arrows T → T′ → T″. The component map is the map at the final object T″, whose lift is bijective. Combine these lifts with the finite-product lemma, first over the second arrow, then over the first arrow, and then over T″, T′, and T in that order.
Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.comparison_degree_zero_bijective: A degree-zero cochain has one component for each object T. The comparison map is the lift of the product of the component maps at these objects. Each objectwise lift is bijective by the objectwise bijectivity lemma. Apply the finite-product lemma to the object index.
Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.liftSemi_cT_bijective: The base-change data at T provides an S-linear equivalence e sending 1 ⊗ b to the image of b under the component map at T. By S-linearity e sends s ⊗ b to s times that image. This is also the value of the objectwise lift on s ⊗ b by the pure tensor formula. The lifts agree on pure tensors and extend additively, so the objectwise lift equals e and is bijective.
Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.liftSemi_piS_bijective: For the finite index set I, tensoring with S over R identifies the tensor product of S with ∏ᵢ Mᵢ with the product ∏ᵢ (S ⊗ Mᵢ). Under this identification the lifted product map is the product of the individual lifted maps. Indeed, on a pure tensor s ⊗ x its i-th component is s · uᵢ(xᵢ) on both sides. The maps are additive, so the identity holds on all tensors. Each component lift is bijective by hypothesis, and their product composed with the tensor-product identification is bijective.
Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.th_bijective: The opposite of the finite poset P has finitely many objects. Each hom-set in its category has at most one element because an arrow is specified by a single order relation. The degree-zero, degree-one, and degree-two comparison lemmas now apply to the given base-change data. Together they prove the three bijectivity assertions.

Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/B.liftSemi_tmul: Through the algebra map R → S, the target is an R-module and the semilinear map f becomes R-linear. The base-change lift extends this map to the tensor product. The extension is S-linear and sends 1 ⊗ x to f(x), so it sends s ⊗ x = s · (1 ⊗ x) to s · f(x).

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.jacobsonSpace_affineSpace: Affine space with finitely many coordinates over k is isomorphic to the spectrum of the polynomial ring in those coordinates. The polynomial ring is a finite-type algebra over a field and therefore is a Jacobson ring. Its spectrum is a Jacobson space, and the homeomorphism induced by the scheme isomorphism transfers this property to affine space.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coprodInitialIsoLeft_hom: The isomorphism from P to the coproduct of the initial scheme and P is built with forward map the inclusion of the second summand. Its inverse is induced by the unique map from the initial scheme and the identity of P.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coprodInitialIsoRight_hom: The isomorphism from P to the coproduct of P and the initial scheme is built with forward map the inclusion of the first summand. Its inverse is induced by the identity of P and the unique map from the initial scheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPullback_comp_inl_coprodDesc: The pullback of the map from F is the initial scheme by the empty-cone criterion. Combine this square with the given pullback square for X using the binary coproduct result. The resulting pullback vertex is the coproduct of P with the initial scheme, canonically isomorphic to P by the first inclusion. Transporting the square through this isomorphism gives the desired maps.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPullback_coprodMap_coprodDesc: Index the two given pullback squares by the two-element set. The finite coproduct pullback result gives the square with indexed coproducts. Identify each indexed coproduct with the binary coproduct by matching the two inclusions. Checking on both summands identifies each arrow with the prescribed binary coproduct map. Transport the pullback property through these isomorphisms.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPullback_initial_of_isEmpty: The maps from the initial scheme form a commuting square because maps from an initial object are unique. Any competing cone has empty underlying space by hypothesis, so its vertex is itself initial in schemes. Thus it has a unique map to the initial scheme, and its composites with the two projections are the original cone maps by uniqueness. This is the pullback universal property.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPullback_of_isPullback_of_iso: Identify X′ with X and P′ with P through the given isomorphisms. The compatibility equations identify the new arrows with the old arrows transported through those isomorphisms. A cone on the new square therefore corresponds to a cone on the old pullback square, with the same unique factorization after transport. This gives the pullback property for the new square.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pairCoprodIso_hom: The comparison isomorphism is constructed with forward map induced by the two inclusions into the indexed coproduct. This is the stated binary coproduct map.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pairInl_comp_desc: By the defining property of the coproduct map, its restriction to the first summand is f₁. Composing with the first inclusion takes this restriction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pairInl_comp_map: The map between the two coproducts is induced by applying the component map and then including its target summand. On the first component this is a₁ followed by the first inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pairInr_comp_desc: The coproduct map is induced by its two stated component maps. Restricting it along the second inclusion gives f₂.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pairInr_comp_map: Restrict the coproduct map to the second summand. By construction that restriction is a₂ followed by the second inclusion of the target coproduct.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sigmaPair_hom_ext: The universal property of the coproduct determines any map out of it from its restrictions to the two summands. The restrictions of f and g agree on both, so f and g are equal.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coe_complOpensOfIsClosed: The complement of the underlying set of C is open by closedness. The indicated open is constructed from this complement, so its underlying set is that complement.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_iso_subscheme_vanishingIdeal_of_c: The open immersion of C is also a closed immersion because its image is the closed set Z. Its defining ideal has support Z, so the vanishing ideal of Z is its radical. Inclusion into that radical factors the vanishing-ideal closed subscheme through C. The factor is a preimmersion and is surjective on points because both immersions into X have image Z and the inclusion of C is injective. Thus the factor is a closed immersion with full support. The scheme C is reduced as an open subscheme of the reduced scheme X. Its only ideal sheaf with full support is zero, since such an ideal is contained in the nilradical. The factor is therefore an isomorphism and its construction gives the stated equality over X.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_iso_subscheme_vanishingIdeal_of_i: Regard the underlying set of C as a closed subset using the given closedness. This closed subset has exactly the same points as C, so apply the comparison of the vanishing-ideal subscheme with the corresponding open subscheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isClosedImmersion_ι_of_isClosed: The inclusion of an open subscheme is an open immersion and hence a preimmersion. Its image is the given open, which is closed by hypothesis. A preimmersion with closed image is a closed immersion.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isIso_sigmaDesc_of_isPullback: The given squares exhibit the C components as the pullbacks of the B coproduct summands along f. Finite coproducts of schemes are stable under this pullback, so the maps from the C components to P make P a coproduct of them. The comparison from their chosen coproduct to P is an isomorphism by uniqueness of coproducts, and it is the map induced by the given component maps.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPullback_sigmaMap_sigmaDesc: Form the pullback of the coproduct map to A along i. The component pullback squares give maps from each C component to this pullback. By pasting with the defining pullback square, the squares over the coproduct inclusions are pullbacks. Stability of the finite coproduct under pullback identifies the coproduct of the C components with the constructed pullback. This identification gives the prescribed maps on each component by construction, so the stated square is a pullback.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_derivation_mul_eq: The derivation D corresponds to a linear map from the differential module over S to S′. Because the module is finitely presented, a common denominator from the multiplicative set clears this linear map. Indeed one can clear denominators on a finite generating set and then multiply by another element of the multiplicative set to kill the images of the finitely many relations. Thus the cleared map comes from a linear map to S. Compose that map with the universal derivation to obtain D₀. Evaluating the cleared equality on each differential gives the asserted formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_derivation_mul_eq_of_isLocalizati: Precompose D with the ring map from S to S′, viewing its values in S′. This is a derivation over R on S. Apply the common denominator result for derivations from S to S′ and evaluate the resulting equality on s.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_liftToLocalization: Factor D through the universal derivation to obtain an S-linear map from the differential module to N. Every element inverted in S′ acts invertibly on N. Thus the linear map extends across the localization of the differential module, which is the differential module of S′ over R. The extension is S′-linear, since the action of each inverted scalar is forced by its inverse. Compose with the universal derivation on S′. Naturality of the universal differential and the extension property show that the result agrees with D on the images of S.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mapToLocalization: Compose D with the localization map on its values, so it becomes a derivation on S with values in S′. Extend this derivation to S′ using the localization property. It then sends an element coming from s to the localization of D(s).
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isUnit_algebraMap_moduleEnd: Multiplication by y on N agrees with the action of its image in S′, which is a unit. Acting by the inverse unit gives the inverse additive map. It is S-linear because scalars from S commute with those from S′, so this is an inverse in the endomorphism ring over S.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.liftToLocalization_algebraMap: The chosen derivation is selected from the extensions of D to the localization. Every extension in this construction takes the image of s to D(s), so the chosen one does as well.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mapToLocalization_algebraMap: The chosen derivation on S′ extends the original derivation with its values mapped to S′. Its evaluation on the image of s is therefore the image of D(s).

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.etale_isZariskiLocalAtSource: Étaleness of a scheme morphism is described on affine neighborhoods by the corresponding property of its ring maps. The locality theorem for morphism properties induced by a local ring-homomorphism property therefore gives Zariski locality on the source.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.etale_sigmaDesc: The open coproduct summands cover the source. The induced morphism restricts on each summand to the given étale morphism. Zariski locality of étaleness on the source gives étaleness of the induced morphism.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.etale_sigmaOpensDesc: Each component map to Y is an open immersion and hence étale. Apply the coproduct result for morphisms that are étale on every component.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_affine_etale_cover_of_isReduced: The structure morphism is quasi-compact, so the inverse image of the quasi-compact whole base makes Y quasi-compact. Choose a finite affine open cover and take the disjoint union W of its members. This union is affine and reduced. Its map to Y is étale on each summand and surjective because the opens cover. Define q by composition with the structure morphism of Y. It is locally of finite type by composition, and it is quasi-compact because W is quasi-compact and the spectrum of the field has one point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_finite_affine_cover: Choose an affine open around each point, giving an open cover. Quasi-compactness supplies a finite subcover. Index the corresponding affine opens by the selected finite set of points. Their union is the whole scheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isAffineOpen_mem: The affine open cover of Y contains the given point in one member. Take the image of that chart, an affine open containing the point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isAffine_sigmaOpens: Each open subscheme is affine by hypothesis. A finite disjoint union of affine schemes is affine, with coordinate ring the finite product of the component rings. Apply this to the given finite family.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isReduced_of_forall_isReduced_stalk: Reducedness of a scheme is equivalent to reducedness of all its local rings. The hypothesis is exactly that pointwise condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isReduced_of_ringEquiv: A nilpotent element maps under the ring isomorphism to a nilpotent element, which is zero in the reduced target. Injectivity then forces the original element to be zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isReduced_sigmaOpens: Any point of the coproduct belongs to one summand. The summand inclusion is an open immersion, so the local ring of the coproduct there is isomorphic to the local ring of that summand. The latter is also the local ring of Y at the corresponding point because the summand is an open subscheme. Since Y is reduced, these local rings are reduced at every point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.locallyOfFiniteType_sigmaOpensDesc: The coproduct map is étale, and every étale morphism is locally of finite presentation and hence locally of finite type.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sigma_ι_sigmaOpensDesc: The map from the coproduct to Y is induced by the open immersions of its summands. Restricting it along the inclusion of the i-th summand recovers the corresponding open immersion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sigma_ι_sigmaOpensDesc_assoc: By associativity, first restrict the coproduct map to the i-th summand. This is the corresponding inclusion into Y, so the further composite is that inclusion followed by h.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.smooth_isZariskiLocalAtSource: Smoothness of scheme morphisms is defined locally through the smoothness of ring maps on affine neighborhoods. The locality theorem for properties induced by local ring-homomorphism properties therefore makes smoothness Zariski-local on the source.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.smooth_sigmaDesc: The coproduct summands form an open cover. The induced map is smooth on each summand because its restriction is the prescribed smooth map there. Source locality gives smoothness on the full coproduct.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.subsingleton_spec_of_field: The only prime ideal of a field is the zero ideal. Any two points of its spectrum therefore coincide.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.surjective_sigmaOpensDesc: A point of Y belongs to one U(i) because the opens cover Y. The corresponding point of that open subscheme gives a point of the coproduct. The coproduct map sends it to the original point by its formula on the i-th summand.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comp_fst_comp_eq_comp_snd_comp_sigmaOpen: The two composites from the pullback to Y agree by commutativity of the pullback square. Precomposing this equality by r gives the claimed identity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.compactSpace_pullback_sigmaOpensDesc: The finite coproduct of the affine opens is affine and hence quasi-compact. The projection from the pullback to this coproduct is quasi-compact by base change of g′. Its inverse image of the whole coproduct is the whole pullback, so the pullback is quasi-compact.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.etale_comp_fst_pullback_sigmaOpensDesc: The first projection is a base change of the étale coproduct map. It is therefore étale, and its composite with the étale map r is étale.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.etale_comp_snd_pullback_sigmaOpensDesc: The second projection is a base change of the given étale morphism g′. Since étale morphisms are preserved by base change and composition, the composite with r is étale.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_affine_etale_cover_pullback_sigma: The scheme W′ is affine and locally of finite type over the field, so g′ is quasi-compact. Its pullback along the coproduct of the affine opens is therefore quasi-compact as a scheme, and the open summand argument makes it reduced. The first projection is étale by base change of the coproduct map, so its composite with q is locally of finite type. This composite is quasi-compact because its source is quasi-compact and the field spectrum has one point. Apply the construction of a reduced affine étale cover to this structure morphism. Its stated factorization is exactly the structure map obtained for the cover.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_sigma_ι_base_eq: The underlying space of the coproduct is the disjoint union of the underlying spaces of the summands. The given point therefore determines an index and a point in that summand, and the summand inclusion sends that point to the given one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isReduced_of_isOpenImmersion_cover: Every point of X lifts to a point of one of the given open immersions. Such an immersion induces an isomorphism on the stalk at that point. The source stalk is reduced by hypothesis, so the target stalk is reduced. As this holds at every point, X is reduced.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isReduced_pullback_sigmaOpensDesc: Pull the open coproduct summands back along the second projection. Their inverse images are open subschemes covering the pullback, since every point of the coproduct belongs to a summand. Each pulled-back summand is canonically the pullback of the corresponding open immersion into Y along g′, hence is an open subscheme of W′. Such an open subscheme is reduced. Reducedness follows on the whole pullback from this open cover.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.quasiCompact_of_compactSpace_to_spec_fie: The spectrum of a field has one point, so a compact open in it is empty or the whole space. Its inverse image is accordingly empty or the whole domain. Both are compact by the hypothesis on the domain, proving quasi-compactness of the map.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.quasiCompact_of_isAffine_of_locallyOfFin: Since the scheme is affine and locally of finite type over the field, its coordinate ring is a finitely generated algebra over the field. It is Noetherian, so its spectrum and hence the scheme are Noetherian topological spaces. Every subset of a Noetherian space is quasi-compact. In particular inverse images of quasi-compact opens under g are quasi-compact.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.surjective_comp_fst_pullback_sigmaOpensD: The coproduct map to Y is surjective because the opens cover Y. Base change makes the first projection surjective. Composing that projection with the surjective map r gives a surjective composite.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.surjective_comp_snd_pullback_sigmaOpensD: The second projection is a base change of the surjective map g′ and is therefore surjective. Its composite with the surjective r remains surjective.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.closure_image_genericPoint: The image of the closure of the singleton of ξ lies in the closure of the singleton of f(ξ) by continuity. Since the former closure is S, closing its image still gives a subset of the latter closed set. Conversely f(ξ) belongs to the image of S, so its singleton closure is contained in the closure of that image.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.closure_inter_open_eq: The closure of S ∩ U is contained in S because S is closed. Conversely any neighborhood of a point in S meets S, and U meets S by hypothesis. Irreducibility of S gives a point in both opens and in S. Thus the neighborhood meets S ∩ U, putting its original point in the closure.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_ι_eq_top_of_disjoint: The support after pulling back along the open immersion is the inverse image of the support of I. The image of the immersion is U, which is disjoint from that support. The inverse image is therefore empty, and an ideal sheaf with empty support is the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isGenericPoint_image_of_isClosedEmbeddin: Since T is the closure of the singleton of y, it is closed, and a closed embedding sends it to a closed set. The image contains f(y), so it contains the closure of that singleton. Continuity sends the image of the closure of y into the closure of the image of y, giving the reverse inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isGenericPoint_preimage_of_isInducing: For an inducing map, the closure of a subset equals the preimage of the closure of its image. Apply this to the singleton of y. Its image is the singleton of ξ, whose closure is T. Thus the singleton of y has closure equal to the preimage of T.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isIrreducible_inter_open: The intersection is nonempty by hypothesis. Two ambient opens meeting the intersection give two open subsets after intersecting each with U. They both meet S, so irreducibility of S gives a point of S lying in both. That point is in the intersection and in both original opens.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isIrreducible_preimage_of_isEmbedding: The preimage is nonempty because T is nonempty and lies in the range. Every open in the domain of the embedding is the inverse image of an ambient open. Two domain opens meeting the preimage of T therefore give two ambient opens meeting T. Their intersection meets T by irreducibility, and the point obtained lifts because T lies in the range. This supplies a point in the required intersection in the domain.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isOpen_sUnion_of_irreducibleComponents: The irreducible components outside C are a finite family of closed sets, so their union is closed. By the disjointness hypothesis no point in the union of C belongs to any such component. Conversely every point off that closed union belongs to an irreducible component, which must belong to C. Thus the two unions are complementary and the union of C is open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_closure_singleton_of_apply: For an open neighborhood O of b, its image is an open neighborhood of f(b). Since f(b) is in the closure of the singleton of f(a), this image contains f(a). Injectivity implies that its preimage point in O is a. Thus every open neighborhood of b contains a, as required.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_comap_eq: The closed support of an ideal sheaf pullback is the inverse image of the original closed support. Taking underlying sets gives exactly the asserted equality.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.irreducibleComponents_eq_of_stalk_isDoma: Let ξ₁ and ξ₂ be the generic points of the two components. Both specialize to x and hence lie in the image of the spectrum of the stalk at x. This spectrum is irreducible because the stalk is a domain. The closure of its image in X is irreducible and contains both generic points, so it contains both of their closures. By maximality of irreducible components each component equals this same irreducible closed subset.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isClosed_sUnion_of_subset_irreducibleCom: A Noetherian space has only finitely many irreducible components, and each is closed. The selected collection is a finite subcollection, so its union is closed.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isOpen_sUnion_of_subset_irreducibleCompo: Every point belongs to an irreducible component. If it lies outside the selected union, any component containing it lies outside the selected collection. Conversely, a point in an unselected component cannot lie in a selected component, since two components meeting at a point agree by hypothesis. The complement is therefore the union of the unselected components. It is closed by finiteness, so the selected union is open.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.algebraMap_tmul_one_eq_one_tmul_algebraM: In either algebra the image of a is its scalar action on one. The balancing relation moves that scalar action across the tensor sign, giving the stated equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.appLE_congr_of_eq: Use the equality of scheme morphisms to identify their pullbacks to the same opens. The maps on sections then agree because they are defined by the same pullback and restriction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.appLE_top_comp_ΓSpecIso_hom: By assumption q factors through the affine open V via the spectrum map of ρ. On affine spectra, pullback on global sections corresponds to the original ring homomorphism under the natural isomorphism between global sections and the coordinate ring. Thus pulling back along q and using that identification yields ρ.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_affineOpen_le_of_mem: Take an affine chart around z. Inside that chart use the principal-open basis to find a neighborhood of z contained in K. A principal open in an affine chart is affine and gives the desired open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_pow_mul_mem_of_map_le: The image of x belongs to the extended ideal of J in the localization. Write it as a fraction whose numerator lies in J and whose denominator is a power of f. Equality with the image of x means the cross-multiplied equality holds after multiplying by some further power of f. Multiplying the powers together gives a power of f times x in J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_eq_of_ideal_affineBasicOpen_eq: On each specified principal open the section ideals are extensions of the original section ideals by localization. Their equality lets us clear a power of its defining element for every element of either ideal to land in the other. Since the defining elements generate the unit ideal, the local membership criterion gives equality of the original ideals.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_eq_of_span_eq_top: Fix x in I. For each f in the generating set, the class of x in the quotient by J is killed by a power of f. The ideal generated by those powers is the unit ideal because its radical contains the original generating set. A finite combination of those powers equals one, so the class of x is zero. This gives I contained in J, and the reverse follows by the same argument with the ideals interchanged.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ker_app_eq_map_ker_of_isPullback_of_flat: The prescribed square commutes, so each section killed by pullback along h maps to a section killed by pullback along h′. This gives one inclusion for the extension of the kernel. Conversely take a section s on V killed by h′. The inverse image of U under h is quasi-compact, so cover it by finitely many affine opens W. On each W the tensor of one with s vanishes by the pullback calculation. The section ring on V is flat over the section ring on U because g is flat. The finite product kernel lemma therefore puts s in the extension of the intersection of the kernels of the maps to the section rings of W. A section in this intersection pulls back to zero on the whole inverse image of U by the sheaf property. Thus the intersection is contained in the kernel of the original pullback, giving the other inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ker_eq_comap_ker_of_isPullback_of_flat: Fix an affine open V in X′. Cover it by principal opens each mapping into an affine open of X. Such opens exist around every point by the affine basis of X and the principal-open basis of V. On each principal open the section ideal of the pulled-back kernel is the extension of the original kernel by the corresponding section map. The affine calculation for flat pullbacks identifies it with the kernel for h′ there. Since these principal opens cover V, the defining sections generate the unit ideal. The local equality criterion for ideals gives equality on V. The two ideal sheaves therefore agree on every affine open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ker_includeRight_eq_map_ker: Let K be the kernel of the map from R to B. The sequence from K into R and then into B is exact at R. Tensoring with A′ preserves exactness because A′ is flat. If x maps to zero under the map to B ⊗ A′, then 1 ⊗ x in R ⊗ A′ comes from K ⊗ A′. Identifying R ⊗ A′ with A′ sends this image into the extended ideal of K, since pure tensors map to products with images of elements of K. Conversely each generator from K maps to zero because its image in B vanishes. Hence the extension of K is exactly the kernel.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lid_rTensor_subtype_mem_map: A pure tensor of k in K with a in A′ maps to the product of the image of k and a in A′. This lies in the extended ideal because the image of k is one of its generators. Every tensor is a finite sum of pure tensors, and the extended ideal is closed under addition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_map_iInf_ker_of_forall_one_tmul_eq_z: Combine the vanishing tensors to obtain vanishing in the tensor product with the finite product of the B factors. The kernel of the map from R to this product is the intersection of the component kernels. The flat tensor kernel formula for the product ring puts s in the extension of this intersection.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.one_tmul_eq_zero_of_app_eq_zero: Form the spectrum of the tensor product of the section rings of W and V over the section ring of U. It maps to Z and X′ through W and V by the two tensor inclusions. The composites to X agree because the two inclusions agree on the base ring, so the maps factor through the scheme pullback. The projection to X′ factors through V. A section s that vanishes under pullback to the preimage of V in the scheme pullback also vanishes upon further pullback to the tensor product spectrum. Its pullback there corresponds to 1 ⊗ s, so this tensor is zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pi_one_tmul_eq_zero_of_forall: Write one in the finite product ring as the sum of the elements supported at just one factor, with value one there. Distribute the tensor over this sum. Each term is the image of the corresponding factor tensor under the linear inclusion of that factor. All such tensors vanish by hypothesis, hence so does their sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.quasiCompact_of_isPullback: In the pullback square, h′ is the base change of h. Quasi-compactness is preserved by base change, so h′ is quasi-compact.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.span_eq_top_of_le_iSup_basicOpen: Identify the affine open with the spectrum of its section ring. A prime containing all the defining sections would belong to none of their basic opens, contradicting the cover. Thus the ideal they generate is contained in no prime and must be the unit ideal.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_ker_comp_subset_support_ker: A section killed by pullback along f remains zero after further pullback along g. Thus the kernel ideal of f is contained in the kernel ideal of the composite. Larger ideals have smaller vanishing supports, giving the claimed containment.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.bijective_appLE_of_image_eq: An open immersion identifies S isomorphically with its open image. The image is O by hypothesis, so pullback gives an isomorphism of the rings of sections over O and S. Its inverse gives a two-sided inverse as a function, proving bijectivity.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isReduced_presheaf_obj_subscheme_ker: On the affine open U the kernel ideal of f is the kernel of pullback on sections. Quotienting by this kernel gives a ring that injects into the section ring on the inverse image in W. That section ring is reduced because W is reduced, and any subring of a reduced ring is reduced. The section ring of the kernel subscheme on its inverse image of U is isomorphic to this quotient.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isReduced_stalk_of_isAffineOpen: The stalk at x in the affine open is the localization of its section ring at the prime of x. Localization preserves reducedness, so the reducedness of the section ring gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isReduced_stalk_subscheme_ker: Choose an affine open U around the image of y in X. Its inverse image in the kernel subscheme is affine because the inclusion is a closed immersion. The ring of sections on that inverse image is reduced by the quotient argument. Localize it at the prime of y to obtain the reduced stalk.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isReduced_subscheme_ker: Apply the stalk computation at each point of the kernel subscheme. Every stalk is reduced, which is the local criterion for the whole scheme to be reduced.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eq_natCast_and_add_one_eq_of_le: The lower bound excludes the bottom element and the upper bound excludes infinity, so a is a finite natural number. The inequalities then give n ≤ a + 1 ≤ d + 1 ≤ n. All bounds are equal, giving a = d and a + 1 = n.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mem_maximalIdeal_notMem_sq_notMem: A Noetherian ring has finitely many minimal primes. If the desired element did not exist, the maximal ideal would be contained in the union of its square and those primes. Prime avoidance applies because every ideal in this finite union except possibly the square is prime. It would place the maximal ideal in its square or in a minimal prime, contrary to the hypotheses.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_repr_ne_zero: If every basis coordinate of v were zero, its basis expansion would be the zero vector. Since v is nonzero, at least one coordinate is nonzero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.false_of_eq_smul_of_linearIndependent: The given equality yields a relation between the two distinct vectors, with coefficient minus one on the j-th vector. This coefficient is nonzero, contradicting linear independence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isDomain: Apply the domain result with the actual finite generator count of the maximal ideal as the bound. The required inequality holds with equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isDomain_of_forall_spanFinrank_lt: If the maximal ideal equals its square, it vanishes by Nakayama’s lemma, so R is a domain. Otherwise the cotangent space is nonzero. If a minimal prime contained the maximal ideal, it would equal it, and all primes would then equal it by minimality and locality. This would give dimension zero, contradicting regularity and the nonzero cotangent space. By prime avoidance choose x in the maximal ideal outside its square and outside all minimal primes. The quotient by x is regular local and its maximal ideal needs fewer generators, so the inductive hypothesis makes it a domain. Thus the principal ideal generated by x is prime and contains some minimal prime p. Any element of p is x times another element. Since p is prime and x lies outside it, the other factor belongs to p. Hence p is contained in its product by the maximal ideal. It is finitely generated, so Nakayama’s lemma makes it zero. The zero ideal is therefore prime and R is a domain.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isDomain_of_maximalIdeal_eq_bot: The maximal ideal of the local ring is prime. If it is zero then the zero ideal is prime, which is equivalent to the ring being a domain.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isDomain_of_spanFinrank_le: Induct on the bound n for the minimum number of generators. For n = 0 there are no smaller generator counts, so the domain criterion with the inductive hypothesis applies vacuously. For a positive bound, any regular local ring with strictly smaller count than that of R has count at most the previous bound. It is a domain by induction. The same criterion then yields that R is a domain.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isLocalRing_quotient_span_singleton: The ideal generated by x lies in the maximal ideal and is therefore proper. The quotient is nonzero. Its maximal ideals correspond to maximal ideals of R containing x, and there is exactly one, since R is local and its maximal ideal contains x. Thus the quotient is local.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPrime_of_mem_minimalPrimes: A minimal prime is a prime ideal minimal among the primes containing zero. In particular it is prime.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPrime_span_singleton: The indicated generator lies in the maximal ideal and has nonzero cotangent class by independence. Quotienting by it gives a regular local ring, which is a domain. A principal ideal with domain quotient is prime.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isRadical_span_singleton_prod: The cotangent independence ensures each principal parameter ideal is prime and each parameter avoids the principal ideal of every other one. The product ideal is therefore the intersection of these principal primes by the product formula. An intersection of prime ideals is radical.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isRegularLocalRing_quotient_span_singlet: Since x lies in the maximal ideal, the quotient is local, and it is Noetherian as a quotient. The dimension calculation identifies its Krull dimension with the minimum number of generators of its maximal ideal. This is the criterion for regularity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_of_le_of_mem_minimalPrimes: The prime q contains zero and lies below the minimal prime p. Minimality forces p to lie below q as well.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.maximalIdeal_eq_bot_of_le_sq: The maximal ideal is finite as a module because the ring is Noetherian. Containment in its square gives equality with its product by the maximal ideal. Nakayama’s lemma then forces the module to be zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.notMem_maximalIdeal_sq: An element of the square of the maximal ideal has zero cotangent class. Linear independence makes each member of the stated family of classes nonzero, so none of its representatives lies in that square.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.notMem_span_singleton: If x(j) lay in the ideal generated by x(i), write it as a ring multiple of x(i). Its cotangent class would then be the residue of that multiplier times the class of x(i). That gives a dependence between the two distinct members of the independent family.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ringKrullDim_quotient_span_singleton_add: The quotient by the element is local since the element lies in the maximal ideal. The dimension calculation for quotienting by an element with nonzero cotangent class gives that its dimension plus one equals the dimension of R.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.spanFinrank_maximalIdeal_quotient_add_on: Write m for the maximal ideal and take a basis of the finite-dimensional cotangent space m/m². The class of x is nonzero, so replace a basis vector at an index with a nonzero coefficient by that class. The resulting family still spans the cotangent space. Lift the unchanged basis vectors to m and take x as the remaining lift. These lifts generate m by Nakayama’s lemma. The maximal ideal of the quotient by x is the image of m, and the image of x vanishes there. Thus it has a generating set with at most one fewer member than the cotangent basis, giving the inequality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.spanFinrank_quotient_eq_ringKrullDim_and: Let d be the minimum number of generators of the maximal ideal of the quotient. Regularity identifies the dimension of R with the dimension of its cotangent space, and the cotangent generator bound gives d + 1 at most this number. The Krull dimension of the quotient is at most d by the general dimension bound for a Noetherian local ring. In the other direction, quotienting by a principal ideal in the maximal ideal lowers Krull dimension by at most one. Thus the dimension of R is at most the quotient dimension plus one, which is at most d + 1, which is at most the dimension of R. Equality throughout gives both claims.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.spanFinrank_span_finset_le_card: The finite set generates its span. The minimum number of generators of that finitely generated ideal is at most the size of any given generating set, in particular the given one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.span_insert_image_erase_eq_top: Every old basis vector except the j-th belongs to the new span. Subtract from v its basis terms at all those other indices. The result is its nonzero j-th scalar times the j-th basis vector. Dividing by that scalar puts the missing basis vector in the span as well, so the span is the whole space.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.toCotangent_mul_eq_smul: The cotangent space is the maximal ideal modulo its square. Its scalar action factors through the residue field because the maximal ideal annihilates this quotient. Thus the class of ra is the class of a multiplied by the residue of r.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isRadical_biInf_span_singleton: An element with a power in the intersection has that power in each of the prime ideals. Each prime ideal is radical, so the element lies in every one of them and therefore belongs to the intersection.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isRadical_span_singleton_prod_finset: The product ideal is the intersection of the principal prime ideals under the stated avoidance condition. Since the intersection of radical ideals is radical, the product ideal is radical.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.list_prod_le_getElem: The product of two ideals is contained in each factor. Apply this first to the head ideal and the product of the tail. For index zero this gives the result directly. For a later index the product lies in the tail product, which lies in the indicated tail ideal by induction. The empty list has no valid index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_eq_map_of_map_eq_map: The two localizations at the same multiplicative set are canonically isomorphic as R-algebras. Extending an ideal of R to T is the same as extending it to S and transporting the result along this isomorphism. Transport the given equality to T.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.prod_notMem_of_isPrime: The complement of a prime ideal is closed under multiplication and contains one. Each of the given factors lies in this complement, so their finite product does too.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.residue_tmul_D_mul_of_mem_maximalIdeal: The Leibniz rule expresses the differential of xc as x times dc plus c times dx. In the residue tensor product the scalars act by their residues. The residue of x is zero because x is in the maximal ideal, leaving the residue of c times the residue tensor of dx.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.span_singleton_mul_eq_inf: The product ab lies in both principal ideals. Conversely, write an element of their intersection as bv. This product lies in the prime ideal generated by a, and b lies outside it, so v belongs to that ideal. Write v as a multiple of a to see that bv is a multiple of ab.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.span_singleton_prod_eq_biInf: Induct on the finite set. The empty product generates the unit ideal, which is the empty intersection. On inserting a new index, the product of the other generators lies outside the prime ideal of the new generator, since each other generator lies outside it. The two-factor formula identifies the product ideal with the intersection of that prime ideal and the ideal of the remaining product. Apply induction to that remaining product.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.algebraMap_basicOpen_eq_presheaf_map: The algebra structure on sections of the basic open is given by restriction from U. Its algebra map is therefore the indicated presheaf restriction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.basicOpen_appLE: Pullback of the basic open of s along f is the basic open of its pulled-back section. Restricting that section further to V intersects its nonvanishing locus with V. This gives the stated intersection.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_affineChart_isStandardSmoothOfRel: Use smoothness of relative dimension r to choose affine neighborhoods of y and its image with standard smooth section map. Find a basic open in the target neighborhood containing the image of y and lying in A₀. Shrink the source neighborhood to the basic open of the pullback of its defining section. This contains y and maps into the chosen target open, and the localized section map remains standard smooth of relative dimension r. Now choose a further basic open in this source neighborhood containing y and lying in B₀. Localizing only the source by this second step again preserves the relative dimension. The resulting affine opens satisfy all the requirements.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.image_preimage_of_le: An image point from the inverse image of A lies in A by definition. Conversely any point of A is in U by hypothesis and therefore is itself the image of a point of the open subscheme U lying above A.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isStandardSmoothOfRelativeDimension_appL: The ring of sections on the basic open of t is the localization of the ring of V at t. The localization map is standard smooth of relative dimension zero. Compose it with the given section map, adding relative dimensions to get n. The composite is the section map into the smaller open, by compatibility with restriction.

Localize the section ring of U at s and the section ring of V at its image. On the given affine opens these are the section rings of the two basic opens. Standard smoothness of relative dimension n is preserved under this localization. The localized ring map equals the pullback on the two basic opens because both agree with the original pullback after restriction, and the localization map is determined by that agreement.
Use the stated equalities to identify the two target opens and the two source opens. Under these identifications the maps on sections are the same, so their standard smoothness properties agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.preimage_comp: A point lies in the inverse image under the composite exactly when its image under f lies in the inverse image of U under g. Thus the two opens have the same points.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.smoothOfRelativeDimension_resLE: At a point of V₀ choose affine neighborhoods inside U₀ and V₀ with a standard smooth section map of relative dimension r. Their inverse images under the two open inclusions are affine and contain the corresponding points. The restricted morphism maps the source neighborhood into the target neighborhood because it agrees with the original morphism after the inclusions. Sections on these inverse-image opens identify with sections on the chosen original opens, and the restricted pullback corresponds to the original section map. Thus it is standard smooth of relative dimension r at every point, which gives the claimed smoothness.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivationOfSurjectiveFun_add: Lift the two target elements to a and b in the source. Their sum lifts to a + b. The formula for the descended function reduces additivity to additivity of D and of f.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivationOfSurjectiveFun_apply: The chosen lift of f(s) has the same image as s. Since the derivation preserves the kernel, the images of the derivatives of the two lifts agree. This gives the formula for the descended function.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivationOfSurjectiveFun_mul: Lift the two elements to x and y. Their product lifts to xy. Apply the Leibniz rule in S and map it to T. The images of the derivatives of the lifts are the descended values, giving the Leibniz rule on T.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivationOfSurjectiveFun_one: Lift the target unit element to one in S. A derivation sends one to zero, so the descended function also sends one to zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivationOfSurjectiveFun_smul: Lift t to a in S. The scalar multiple of a lifts the corresponding scalar multiple of t because f is a k-algebra map. Apply k-linearity of D and of f to the formula for the descended function at this lift.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivationOfSurjective_apply: The descended derivation has the same underlying function used in its construction. Its value at f(s) is the image of D(s) by the formula for evaluating that function on a lift.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_derivation_eq_of_map_eq: If s and s′ have the same image, their difference lies in the kernel. The derivation preserves this kernel, so the derivative of their difference has zero image. Additivity gives equality of the images of their derivatives.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_add: Induct on r. At zero the equality follows from the identity iterate. Increasing r by one applies the derivative ideal operation to both sides of the equality for r. The recursive definition identifies these with the two sides at the successor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_le_of_le: Write r′ as r plus a nonnegative difference. The addition law expresses the r′-th iterate as the additional iterations applied to the r-th iterate. Iteration contains its starting ideal, giving the inequality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_le_pow_of_le_pow: Induct on the iteration count. At zero the result is the given containment. For the successor, use monotonicity to put the next derivative ideal in the derivative ideal of the current upper power. The one-step estimate lowers that exponent by one with truncation at zero. This is the exponent n minus the new iteration count.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_one: One iteration applies the derivative ideal operation to the zero-th iterate, which is J itself.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_succ: The recursion defines the successor iterate by applying the derivative ideal operation once to the previous iterate. This is the stated equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_zero: Zero iterations apply the identity to J by the definition of iteration.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_bot: The only element of the zero ideal is zero, and every derivation takes zero to zero. Every generator of the resulting derivative ideal is therefore zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_eq_sup_span: The derivative ideal is defined as the sum of J and the span of the values of all base-linear derivations on elements of J. This is exactly the expression in the statement.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_iSup_le: The sum of the original family lies in the sum of its derivative ideals because each original ideal lies in its own derivative ideal. The sum of the originals is generated by their union. Every derivative of an element of this union lies in the derivative ideal of a corresponding member, and hence in the sum of the derivative ideals. The span argument extends that containment to derivatives of the whole sum. The containment criterion gives the claim.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_le_derivIdeal: Apply monotonicity of the derivative ideal operation to the inclusion of I in J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_le_iff: The derivative ideal is generated by J and all indicated derivative values. It lies in K exactly when K contains the first summand and contains each generator of the second summand. These are the two stated conditions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_le_pow_of_le_pow: Monotonicity puts the derivative ideal of I in the derivative ideal of the n-th power of P. The power estimate bounds the latter by the power with exponent n − 1, with exponent zero when n is zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_mono: If I is contained in J, every element of I belongs to the derivative ideal of J. Every derivative of an element of I belongs there as well, since the element is in J. The ideal containment criterion therefore gives monotonicity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_mul_le: The product IJ lies in the first summand on the right because J lies in its derivative ideal. The product ideal is additively generated by products of one element from each factor. By the Leibniz rule the derivative of a product is the sum of a term belonging to the first summand and a term belonging to the second. Additivity puts every derivative of the product ideal in their sum, proving the claim.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_pow_le: For n equal to zero, the target is the unit ideal because the exponent is truncated at zero. For n positive apply the containment of the derivative ideal of a successor power in the preceding power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_pow_succ_le: The original power is J to the n-th power times J, and J lies in its derivative ideal. Every derivative of the original power also belongs to the stated product by the derivative estimate for powers. Apply the ideal containment criterion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_pow_succ_le_pow: The original power is contained in the preceding power because it is that power multiplied by J. Its derivative values are contained there as well by the Leibniz estimate. These two containments suffice by the definition of the derivative ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_top: The derivative ideal contains its input ideal. When the input is the unit ideal, this containment forces equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_apply_mem_derivIdeal: The element D(x) is one of the generators adjoined to J in the derivative ideal, since x belongs to J. It therefore lies in that ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_apply_mem_of_mem_span: Induct through the ideal span. The derivative of every chosen generator belongs to T by hypothesis, and the derivative of zero is zero. Additivity handles sums. For a multiple ab of an element b already in the span, the Leibniz rule writes its derivative as a times the derivative of b plus b times the derivative of a. The first term is in T by induction and the second because b is in T. Thus every element of the span has derivative in T.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_apply_mem_pow_mul_derivIdeal: Induct on n. At zero every derivative of J lies in its derivative ideal. For the successor step write elements of the power as sums of products of an element from the previous power and an element of J. Differentiating the J factor gives a member of the derivative ideal of J multiplied by the previous power. Differentiating the other factor uses induction, and multiplication by the remaining J factor restores the exponent required on the right. Additivity extends the estimate to the sums.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_apply_mem_pow_of_mem_pow_succ: Induct on n. For n equal to zero the target is the unit ideal. At a successor, use additivity to reduce to a product of an element of the previous power and an element of J. In the Leibniz term differentiating the J factor, the other factor already belongs to the desired power. In the term differentiating the other factor, its derivative belongs to the power one smaller by induction, and the remaining factor of J restores the desired power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_derivIdeal: The derivative ideal is a sum of ideals one of whose summands is J. Therefore it contains J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_derivIdealIterate: At zero the iterate equals J. Each new iterate contains the previous one because the derivative ideal contains its input. Repeated inclusion gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pow_succ_le_pow: A product of an element of the m-th power and an element of J belongs to the m-th power, since it is an ideal. The products generate the next power, giving the containment.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.algebraMap_comp_derivation_apply: The derivation with values in T is constructed by applying the structure map to every value of the original derivation. Its value at s is the image of the original value at s.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_comp_algebraMap_apply: The restricted derivation is constructed by precomposing the given derivation with the structure map from S to T. Evaluating this composite on s gives the asserted value.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_ext_of_coord: Each derivation factors through a linear map on the differential module. The coordinate differentials form a basis by formal étaleness. The hypothesis gives equality of the two linear maps on every basis vector, hence on the whole module. Composing with the universal differential gives equality of the derivations.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_derivIdeal_sum: The old partial derivations span all derivations of S.
