After applying the structure map, each of their values on J is a value of the corresponding partial derivation in T on the extended ideal. This gives containment of the extended derivative ideal in the new derivative ideal. Conversely the partial derivations in T span all derivations there. The partials for old coordinates give images of original derivatives on elements from J, and partials for extra coordinates give zero on those images. Thus all derivatives of the generators of the extended J lie in the extended derivative ideal. The Leibniz rule extends this to the ideal they generate, because that ideal is itself contained in the extended derivative ideal. This gives the other containment.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDeriv_inl_algebraMap: Compare the partial derivation for the old coordinate in T restricted to S with the corresponding partial derivation in S followed by the structure map on its values. Both take one on the indicated coordinate and zero on all the other coordinates of S. Since coordinate values determine a derivation, these maps agree on every s.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDeriv_inr_algebraMap: Restrict the partial derivation for the extra coordinate j to S. On each coordinate of S it vanishes, since that coordinate maps to a coordinate in the first block. Derivations on S are determined by the coordinate values, so the restricted derivation is zero.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.apply_mem_of_forall_partialDeriv_mem: The derivations whose values on X lie in K form a submodule because evaluation is linear and K is an ideal. By hypothesis each partial derivation belongs to this submodule. The partial derivations span the module of derivations, so all derivations belong to it, including D.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_map_le: The extension of J lies in the extension of its derivative ideal. All coordinate partial derivatives on the extended J belong to the latter ideal by the generator argument. They span all derivations over L, so the same containment holds for every derivative of every element of the extended J. Apply the derivative ideal containment criterion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_derivIdeal: The coordinate compatibility gives one inclusion by transporting the source partial derivatives. It gives the reverse by applying the target partial derivatives to generators of the extended ideal and then extending to all derivatives. The two containments give equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_derivIdeal_le: Each element of J maps into the extended J and hence into its derivative ideal over L. For each source coordinate partial derivation, its value on J maps to the value of the corresponding partial derivation over L on the image of that element. These images therefore belong to the desired ideal. Since coordinate partial derivations span all source derivations, this holds for every derivative generator. The extended derivative ideal is generated by these images together with the images of J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDeriv_algHom_apply: View each side as the value at f of a k-derivation from S to S′. On the left, the partial derivation over L is restricted to S through φ and is k-linear because the scalar map from k factors through L. On the right, apply φ to the values of the partial derivation over k. Since φ sends coordinates to the corresponding coordinates, both derivations have the same dual values on every coordinate of S. The coordinate differentials are a basis, so these derivations coincide.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDeriv_mem_map_derivIdeal: The extended J is generated by the images of elements of J, and all those images lie in the extended derivative ideal. The chosen target partial derivative of any such generator is the image of the corresponding source partial derivative and so belongs to the extended derivative ideal. The Leibniz rule and additivity extend this membership from the generators to every element of the extended J.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_map_le: The extended ideal itself lies in the extension of the derivative ideal. Any element x of the extended ideal is a fraction with numerator a from J and a denominator m that becomes a unit. For a derivation of the localization, the Leibniz rule on mx = a gives m² times the derivative of x as m times the derivative of a minus a times the derivative of m, with all elements read in the localization. The first term is in the extended derivative ideal by the cleared-derivation lemma, and the second belongs there because a lies in the extended original ideal. Cancel the unit m twice. The derivative ideal containment criterion gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_algebraMap_mem_map_derivIdeal: Since the differential module is finitely presented, clear a common denominator of the restricted derivation to obtain a derivation of S with values in S. The cleared derivative of a is then the image of a derivative of an element of J, so it lies in the extended derivative ideal. The denominator acts by a unit in the localization, and canceling it proves membership of the original derivative.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_derivIdeal: The extension of the original derivative ideal is contained in the derivative ideal of the extension by extending derivations. Finite presentation of the differential module gives the reverse containment by clearing denominators. Therefore the two ideals agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_derivIdeal_away: Localization away from g is localization at the multiplicative set of its powers. Apply the equality for a general localization to that set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_derivIdeal_le: The extension of J is contained in its derivative ideal. Each original derivation extends to the localization and agrees there on the images of elements of S. Thus the image of every derivative generator for J is a derivative of an element of the extended ideal. This proves containment for all the generators of the extended derivative ideal.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eq_natCast_of_le_of_not_succ_le: The upper condition excludes infinity. For the resulting ordinary natural number, being at least n and strictly below n + 1 forces equality with n.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eulerDerivation_apply: The Euler derivation is the sum of the coordinate derivations with the given coefficients. Apply the finite-sum evaluation formula over the full index set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eulerDerivation_apply_generator: On the chosen generator the duality hypothesis makes every summand vanish except the one at the matching index. That term is the generator itself multiplied by one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eulerDerivation_apply_mem_span: In the Euler sum each term has a coordinate generator as a factor and therefore belongs to the coordinate ideal. The sum belongs to the ideal as well.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eulerDerivation_sub_natCast_mul_mem_pow_: Apply the Euler congruence for the r-th power of the coordinate ideal to the given element f.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eulerDerivation_sub_self_mem_sq: Let J be the coordinate ideal. On each generator, the Euler derivation gives the generator itself. The difference between the Euler value and the input is additive. For a multiple ca of an element of J, this difference is c times the difference for a plus a times the Euler value of c, by the Leibniz rule. The latter term lies in J² because every Euler value lies in J. Induction on expressions in the ideal span gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.forall_eulerDerivation_sub_natCast_mul_m: Let J be the coordinate ideal and induct on r. At zero every Euler value lies in J. At the successor, use sums of products ab with a in the r-th power and b in J. Write E for the Euler derivation. By the Leibniz rule, E(ab) − (r + 1)ab equals a(E(b) − b) + b(E(a) − ra). The first difference lies in J² and the second lies in the (r + 1)-st power by induction. Both products lie in the (r + 2)-nd power, and additivity gives the claim for all sums.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_derivIdealIterate_of_isUnit_n: Induct on j. At zero the iterate is I and the order is r. For a successor within the bound j + 1 ≤ r, the preceding iterate has order r − j, which is positive. Applying the one-step decrease gives order r − j − 1, the required order at the successor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_derivIdeal_of_isUnit_natCast: Order r means I lies in the r-th power of the maximal ideal and fails to lie in the next power. The general derivative estimate puts the derivative ideal in the (r − 1)-st power. The Euler argument with r a unit shows that the derivative ideal cannot lie in the r-th power, because the parameters generate the maximal ideal. These two facts give order exactly r − 1.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_pow_succ_of_deriv_mem_pow: Each term in the Euler value of f is a generator times a derivative lying in the r-th power. Thus the Euler value lies in the next power. By the Euler congruence it differs from r times f by another element of that next power. Subtract to put r times f in the next power, then multiply by the inverse of r to obtain f there.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.not_derivIdeal_le_pow: If the entire derivative ideal lay in the r-th power, then each dual derivation of every element of I would take values in that power. Since the elements of I already lie in that power and r is a unit, the Euler criterion puts every one of them in the next power. This contradicts the failure of that containment.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_smul_derivation_apply: Evaluation at a commutes with finite sums of derivations because their addition is pointwise. Evaluating a scalar multiple multiplies the value by the same ring element, giving the stated sum.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.algebraMap_sectionsAlgebra: The algebra structure is defined by the given ring homomorphism from k to the section ring. Its structure homomorphism is therefore that same map.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheafIterate_add: Induct on r. At zero the outer iterate is the identity. At each successor apply the derivative ideal sheaf operation to both sides of the induction equality, which gives the new equality by the recursion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheafIterate_ideal: At zero both sides are the original section ideal. At a successor the sheaf operation on the previous iterate takes its affine section ideal to the ring-level derivative ideal. By induction the input is the previous ring-level iterate, so its derivative ideal is the next ring-level iterate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheafIterate_one: One iteration applies the derivative ideal sheaf operation to the zero-th iterate, which is I.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheafIterate_succ: The successor iterate is defined by applying the derivative ideal sheaf operation to the preceding iterate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheafIterate_zero: The zero-th iterate is the original ideal sheaf by definition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheaf_ideal: The derivative ideal sheaf assigns to each affine open the derivative ideal of its original ideal in the section ring, using the k-algebra structure induced by the structural morphism.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheaf_map_ideal_basicOpen: Restriction of sections from an affine open to the basic open is localization at f and respects the scalar maps from k. The ideal on the basic open is the extension of the original section ideal. The differential module of the original section ring is finitely presented, so the derivative ideal commutes with this localization. This identifies the extended derivative ideal with the derivative ideal assigned to the basic open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheaf_mono: An inclusion of ideal sheaves yields inclusions of the section ideals on all affine opens. The ring-level derivative ideal is monotone, so it preserves each inclusion. These inclusions give monotonicity of the sheaf operation.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheaf_mul_le: On an affine open, multiplication of ideal sheaves gives the product of their section ideals. Apply the product bound for the derivative ideal of that ring product. The two terms on the right are the section ideals of the two product sheaves, each of which lies in the section ideal of their sum. This proves the claim on every affine open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheaf_pow_succ_le: On each affine open the power and products of ideal sheaves are the corresponding operations on the section ideals. Applying the derivative ideal bound for a successor power to those ideals gives the asserted containment there, and hence globally.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.finitePresentation_kaehlerDifferential_s: The section ring is of finite type over k, so its differential module is generated by the differentials of finitely many algebra generators. The section ring is Noetherian. Over such a ring a finite module is finitely presented, giving the claim.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.finiteType_sections: Since the morphism is locally of finite type, its ring map from the affine base to the sections on U is of finite type. The global sections of the affine base identify with k. Composing with this identification preserves finite type, and the given algebra structure uses exactly the resulting scalar map.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isNoetherianRing_sections: The section ring is a finitely generated algebra over the Noetherian ring k. The Hilbert basis theorem therefore makes the section ring Noetherian.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isScalarTower_sections: The scalar maps from k are the pullbacks of global sections of the base. The structure map between the two section rings is restriction. Restriction sends the scalar section on U to the same scalar section on the basic open, showing that the two routes from k agree. This is the scalar tower condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_derivIdealSheaf: On every affine open the derivative ideal of the section ideal contains the section ideal itself. These containments give the inclusion of ideal sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_derivIdealSheafIterate: At zero the iterate equals I. Each new derivative ideal sheaf contains the previous one, so induction gives containment of I in every iterate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_preimage_top: The inverse image of the whole base is the whole source, which contains U.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sectionsAlgebraMap_comp_restrict: Pullback of global sections to an open, followed by restriction to a smaller open, equals direct pullback to the smaller open. Composing this equality with the identification of k with the base global sections gives the stated compatibility.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sectionsAlgebraMap_eq: The structure map on sections first identifies k with the global sections of its spectrum. It then pulls these sections back to U along the structural morphism. This is the defining composite.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sectionsAlgebraMap_restrict_apply: Evaluate the compatibility of the two structure maps with restriction at the scalar a.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheafIterate_comap: At zero both sides are the pullback of I. At each successor, apply the induction equality for the preceding iterate and then use the one-step result that the derivative ideal sheaf commutes with smooth pullback.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheaf_comap: At every point of Y the local smooth charts give an affine neighborhood where the two section ideals agree. Equality of ideal sheaves is local, so these affine equalities give the claimed equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_affineOpen_derivIdealSheaf_comap_: Choose an étale chart around the image of y in X. Smoothness of h gives affine neighborhoods W of that image and V of y where h admits an étale chart over relative affine space over W. Shrink W inside the original chart and restrict it. The section ring of W is formally étale over the polynomial ring in its original coordinates. The section ring of V is formally étale over the polynomial ring over the sections of W in the relative coordinates. Composing gives formal étaleness over the polynomial ring over k in both sets of coordinates, where the original coordinates map to the corresponding first set. On V, pullback of each ideal sheaf extends its ideal on W along the section map. The ring-level equality for compatible old and new coordinates identifies the derivative ideal of the extended ideal with the extension of its original derivative ideal. This is the required equality on V.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_pow_mul_mem_of_mem_map: Represent the image of x as a fraction with numerator in N and denominator a power of f. Equality in the localization implies equality after multiplying the cross-multiplied expressions by a further power of f. The resulting product of powers times x belongs to N.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_eq_of_locally_eq: The local equalities give local containments in both directions. Apply the result that local affine containments imply containment on each affine open. The two ideals thus agree on every affine open, which gives equality of the ideal sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_ideal_le_congr: Identify the affine opens by the given equality. The two section rings and their ideal values then coincide, and the stated inclusion transfers.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_ideal_le_of_locally_le: Fix an element x of the ideal of the first sheaf on U. At every point of U choose an affine neighborhood where the local containment holds, then shrink to a common neighborhood principal in both affines. Ideal extension along the restriction preserves that local containment. Thus on the principal open in U the image of x lies in the localized ideal of the second sheaf. Clearing a power of the defining section puts a multiple of x in the second ideal on U. The defining sections of these principal opens generate the unit ideal because the opens cover U. The powers that kill the class of x modulo the second ideal also generate the unit ideal, so that class is zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sectionsAlgebraMap_appLE_apply: Evaluate the compatibility of scalar maps with pullback at a.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sectionsAlgebraMap_comp_appLE: Sending a scalar first to W via p and then to V via h pulls the same base global section back along the composite morphism. Functoriality of pullback and restriction identifies this with the structure map for the composite on V.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.add_idealOrder_le_idealOrder_mul: For any finite m and n bounded by the orders of I and J, the two ideals lie in the corresponding powers of the maximal ideal. Their product therefore lies in the power with exponent m + n. Hence every such sum is bounded by the order of the product. The extended-natural addition criterion gives the inequality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.enat_add_le_of_forall_natCast_add_le: If either a or b is infinite, take the finite bound on that argument arbitrarily large and take zero on the other. The hypothesis then makes c infinite, giving the inequality. If both are finite, take their actual values as m and n and apply the hypothesis.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_idealOrder_eq_coe: A nonzero ideal of a Noetherian local ring has order different from infinity by the Krull intersection argument. Every finite extended natural number is represented by an ordinary natural number.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_bot: The zero ideal is contained in every power of the maximal ideal. The criterion for infinite order therefore applies.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_eq_top_iff: An extended natural number is infinite exactly when it is at least every natural number. Apply the finite-exponent criterion to each such lower bound to get the equivalent ideal containments.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_eq_zero_iff: An extended natural number is zero exactly when it is less than one. By the order-one criterion, failure of order at least one is equivalent to failure of containment in the maximal ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_le_idealOrder_map: Take any finite exponent bounded by the order of I. Extend the containment of I in that power of the source maximal ideal. The image of this power lies in the corresponding power of the target maximal ideal, so the same exponent is bounded by the order of the extended ideal. Comparing all finite lower bounds gives the claim.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_le_of_le: If a power of the maximal ideal contains J, it also contains I because I is contained in J. The set of exponents defining the order of J is therefore contained in the set defining the order of I. Taking suprema gives the inequality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_ne_top_of_ne_bot: If the order were infinite, the ideal would lie in every power of the maximal ideal. Their intersection is zero by the Krull intersection theorem for Noetherian local rings. This would make the ideal zero, contrary to the hypothesis.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_sup: The sum of the ideals is contained in a given power of the maximal ideal exactly when both summands are contained in that power. Thus an ordinary exponent is at most the order of the sum precisely when it is at most both individual orders. These finite lower bounds determine the extended order, so it is the minimum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_top: The unit ideal is not contained in the proper maximal ideal, so the order-zero criterion gives order zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_idealOrder_iff: If I is contained in the n-th power of the maximal ideal, then n occurs in the set defining its order and hence is at most the supremum. Conversely, if that containment fails, n is positive because the zeroth power is the unit ideal. The powers are decreasing, so every exponent for which containment holds is less than n. Their supremum is at most n − 1, contradicting the assumed lower bound.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_maximalIdeal_pow_le_pow: Extension of ideals commutes with ideal products. For exponent zero the inequality is automatic because the target is the unit ideal. At a successor use the product formula, the previous inequality for the lower power, and the assumed containment for the image of the maximal ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_idealOrder_le_idealOrder_pow: For exponent zero the lower bound is zero. For a positive exponent, if I has infinite order then its power is contained in I and also has infinite order. If the order of I is finite, say n, then I lies in the n-th power of the maximal ideal. Taking c-th powers yields containment in the power with exponent cn, which gives the bound.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.one_le_idealOrder_iff: Apply the finite-exponent criterion at one. The first power of the maximal ideal is the maximal ideal itself.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.one_le_idealOrder_iff_ne_top: Order at least one is equivalent to containment in the maximal ideal. Every proper ideal of a local ring lies in the maximal ideal, and any ideal contained there is proper. This gives the equivalence.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_ofDigits_le_of_sum_eq: The tuples of degree r form a finite set because each coordinate lies between zero and r. Its subset satisfying P is nonempty. Choose a member of that subset minimizing the weighted digit value.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_eq_of_le_of_not_le: The two containments for successive powers translate to order at least n and order strictly below n + 1. An extended natural number between those bounds is exactly n.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_mul: If either ideal is zero the product is zero and both sides are infinite. Otherwise let r and s be the finite orders of I and J. Their product lies in the (r + s)-th power of the maximal ideal. Choose an element of each ideal failing to lie in the power one higher than its order. The nonvanishing result for the product of their leading terms gives an element of IJ outside the (r + s + 1)-st power. The two power bounds imply that the order is exactly r + s.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_pow: At exponent zero the power is the unit ideal, with order zero. At a successor the next power is the previous power multiplied by I. Apply the order formula for a product and use induction to obtain the stated multiple.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_maximalIdeal_pow_succ_iff_multiIndex: If f lies in the (r + 1)-st power, every derivative of order r lies in the maximal ideal by the power bound for mixed derivatives. For the converse, the finite index set contains all multi-indices of degree r. The vanishing criterion proved by induction and the Euler argument then puts f in the next power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_maximalIdeal_pow_succ_of_multiIndexD: Induct on r. At zero the only required derivative is the identity, so f already lies in the maximal ideal. For a step from r to r + 1, each first derivative of f lies in the r-th power. Its derivatives of total order r are derivatives of f of total order r + 1 because the coordinate derivations commute. They therefore vanish in the residue field. By induction every first derivative of f lies in the (r + 1)-st power. Apply the Euler congruence in degree r + 1 and use the invertibility of r + 1 to conclude that f lies in the (r + 2)-nd power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_multiIndicesOfDegree: The definition keeps precisely the bounded multi-indices of total degree r. If the sum is r, then every entry is at most r because the entries are nonnegative. Thus the bound in the definition follows from the degree condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_notMem_maximalIdeal_pow_add_succ: By the mixed-derivative criterion choose degree r and degree s derivatives of f and g with nonzero residues. Among such indices for each factor choose indices β₀ and γ₀ of minimal weighted digit value in base r + s + 1. Let α be their coordinatewise sum. The residue of the α-th derivative of the product is given by the mixed Leibniz sum over splits α = β + γ of degrees r and s, since all other splits vanish modulo the maximal ideal. For the selected split both derivatives and the positive binomial coefficient are units, so its term survives. For any other split whose first derivative survives, the value of β is strictly larger than that of β₀ by minimality and uniqueness of the base representation. Additivity of the weighted values then makes the value of γ strictly smaller than that of γ₀, so its derivative vanishes. Thus the selected term is the only nonzero residue and the α-th derivative does not vanish. The power bound on derivatives excludes membership of the product in the (r + s + 1)-st power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ofDigits_add: The weighted sum defining the digit value distributes over coordinatewise addition. Splitting the finite sum gives the sum of the two digit values.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ofDigits_fin_succ: The first digit has weight one. Each tail weight is the corresponding weight for the shortened tuple multiplied by N. Separate the first term and factor out N from the tail.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ofDigits_injective_of_lt: Induct on the number of digits. For a nonempty tuple compare the two values modulo N. This identifies the first digits because they are less than N. Subtract this common digit and cancel the positive factor N to identify the tail values. The induction hypothesis identifies all the remaining digits.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_notMem_of_unique_notMem: The sum of all terms except the distinguished one belongs to I. If the whole sum belonged to I as well, subtracting that sum of the remaining terms would put the distinguished term in I, a contradiction.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_apply_mem_logDerivIdeal: The given derivation preserves P and the input belongs to J. Its value is therefore one of the generators of the logarithmic derivative ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_logDerivIdeal: The logarithmic derivative ideal contains J because J is one summand in its definition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_logDerivIdealIterate: Every application contains the ideal to which it is applied. Starting with J at iteration zero and composing these inclusions proves the claim.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_add: Induct on r. At zero the composition with the zero-th iterate changes nothing. The successor applies the logarithmic derivative ideal operation once more to both sides of the induction equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_iSup_le: At zero both sides are the sum of the original ideals. At a successor, apply the logarithmic derivative ideal operation to the induction containment using monotonicity. The one-step sum estimate then bounds the result by the sum obtained by applying the operation to each individual iterate. This is the desired sum at the successor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_le_of_le: Write r′ as r plus a nonnegative difference. The iteration law expresses the larger iterate as the additional iterations applied to the r-th iterate. These additional iterations contain their starting ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_mono: At zero the operation is the identity and is monotone. At a successor it is the composition of the previous monotone iterate and the monotone logarithmic derivative ideal operation. Induction gives monotonicity at every count.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_one: The first iterate is the logarithmic derivative ideal of the zero-th iterate, which is J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_succ: At a successor the recursive definition applies the logarithmic derivative ideal operation to the previous iterate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_top_eq_derivIdealIt: At zero both iterates are J. When P is the unit ideal, one application of the logarithmic operation equals one application of the ordinary operation. Apply this equality at each successor step to obtain equality of the iterates.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_zero: By definition zero applications of the operation return the original ideal J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_eq_sup_span: The logarithmic derivative ideal is defined as the sum of J and the ideal generated by derivatives of its elements under derivations preserving P.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_iSup_le: Each J(i) lies in its own logarithmic derivative ideal, so their sum lies in the sum of these enlarged ideals. For a fixed tangent derivation, derivatives of elements from each J(i) lie in its enlarged ideal. Every element of the sum is a finite sum of elements from these ideals, and additivity then puts its derivative in the sum of the enlarged ideals. The containment criterion gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_le_derivIdeal: The ordinary derivative ideal contains J and the derivatives of its elements under all derivations. Among those are the derivations preserving P. Thus it contains every generator of the logarithmic derivative ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_le_iff: The logarithmic derivative ideal is the sum of J and the span of the permitted derivative values. It is contained in K exactly when both summands are contained there. For the span, this means precisely that every stated derivative value belongs to K.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_le_logDerivIdeal: Apply monotonicity for the fixed ideal P to the given inclusion from I to J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_mono: If I is contained in J, every element of I is in the logarithmic derivative ideal of J. Every permitted derivative value from I is also a permitted derivative value from J. The containment criterion gives monotonicity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_top_eq_derivIdeal: Every derivation preserves the unit ideal because all ring elements belong to it. The permitted derivatives in the logarithmic construction are therefore all the derivatives used in the ordinary construction. Both ideals also contain the same original generators.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_tangentDerivations: The tangent derivations are defined to be those that take every element of P back into P. Membership is therefore exactly the stated condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_tangentDerivations_span_singleton: A tangent derivation must take the generator x into its principal ideal. Conversely, if that value belongs to the ideal, then the Leibniz rule puts the derivative of every multiple of x in the same ideal. These multiples are all of its elements.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.smul_mem_tangentDerivations: At an element x of P, the scaled derivation takes the value p times D(x). This belongs to P because p belongs to the ideal and ideals absorb multiplication by arbitrary ring elements.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_mem_map_of_forall_mem: The extended ideal is generated by the images of elements of P. Their derivatives lie in the extended ideal by hypothesis. Additivity and the Leibniz rule extend this to the whole span because multiplying a generator or another element of that ideal by a derivative still gives an element of the ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_smul_apply: Scalar multiplication of derivations is defined by multiplying their values. Thus evaluation at x gives c times the original derivative.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mem_mul_algebraMap_eq_of_mem_map: An element of an extended ideal in a localization can be written as a fraction with numerator in the original ideal and denominator in the inverted multiplicative set. Multiplying this expression by its denominator gives the displayed equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mem_tangentDerivations_mul_eq: Finite presentation of the differential module clears a common denominator of the restricted derivation, yielding a derivation D₀ of S. Choose finitely many generators of P. Since the original localized derivation preserves the extended P, the image of the value of D₀ on each generator lies in that ideal. For each generator clear another denominator to put that value into P in the source. Multiply these finitely many denominators to get one factor c that works for all generators. The scaled derivation cD₀ then preserves all of P by the Leibniz rule. It agrees with the given derivation on source elements after multiplying by the product of c and the first denominator.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mul_mem_of_algebraMap_mem_map: Write the localized image of y as a fraction with numerator p in P and denominator t from the multiplicative set. The images of ty and p agree in the localization. Some further denominator c therefore gives equality of their products with c in the original ring. Hence cty is a multiple of p and lies in P, and ct belongs to the multiplicative set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_map: At zero both sides are the extension of J. At a successor apply the equality for a single logarithmic derivative ideal, with the previous iterate as input. The induction equality identifies that extended input with the previous iterate after localization.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_map_away: Localization away from g is localization at its powers. Apply the iterated localization formula to that multiplicative set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_map: Extending source tangent derivations proves one inclusion. Clearing denominators using the finite generation of P and finite presentation of the differential module gives the other inclusion. The resulting ideals are equal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_map_away: Use the multiplicative set of powers of g in the formula for localization of a logarithmic derivative ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_map_le_map_logDerivIdeal: The extension of J already lies in the extension of its logarithmic derivative ideal. Let D preserve the extension of P and take x in the extension of J. Clear a unit denominator m so that on source elements mD is the image of a derivation D₁ preserving P. Choose a numerator y in J and denominator t with tx equal to the image of y. Apply the Leibniz rule to tx and multiply by m. This expresses mtD(x) as the image of D₁(y) minus x times the image of D₁(t). The first term belongs to the extended logarithmic derivative ideal by tangency of D₁, and the second belongs because x lies in the extended J. Since mt is a unit after localization, D(x) belongs to the desired ideal. This establishes containment for the localized logarithmic derivative ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mapToLocalization_mem_tangentDerivations: An extended derivation agrees with the original derivation on the images of source elements. For each p in P, the derivative of its image is therefore the image of an element of P. The extended ideal is generated by these images, and the Leibniz rule extends the containment from the generators to that entire ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdeal_le: The images of J lie in the localized logarithmic derivative ideal. A derivation preserving P extends to the localization and preserves the extension of P. Its derivative on the image of an element of J is the image of the original derivative. Every generator of the extended logarithmic derivative ideal therefore belongs to the localized one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_derivation_mem_of_span_eq: The scaled derivation has values in P on the given generators. It preserves sums, and its value on a multiple of an element of P is a multiple of that element’s derivative plus a multiple of the element itself. Thus the property extends to all of P by the span property.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdealIterate_ker_le_derivIde: At the zero-th iterate both sides give the extended J. At a successor apply the one-step quotient containment to the preceding logarithmic iterate. The induction hypothesis and monotonicity of the target derivative ideal bound the result by the next ordinary iterate of the extended J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdealIterate_le_derivIdealIt: Replace P by the kernel of f using the assumed equality. The iterative quotient containment then gives exactly the stated result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdeal_ker_le_derivIdeal_map: The images of the elements of J belong to the ordinary derivative ideal of its extension. A derivation preserving the kernel of f descends through the surjection. Thus the image of its derivative of an element of J is the derivative of the corresponding image under the descended derivation. It belongs to the target derivative ideal as well. This gives the containment on all generators.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_add: Induct on r. At zero the outer iterate is the identity. At a successor apply one more logarithmic derivative step to both sides and use the recursive definition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_ideal: At zero both sides are the original section ideal. At a successor take the sections of the logarithmic derivative ideal sheaf of the preceding iterate. This applies the ring operation to the section ideal at the previous step, which is the preceding ring-level iterate by induction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_le_derivIdealS: At zero the two iterates agree. At a successor the logarithmic derivative sheaf of the previous logarithmic iterate lies in its ordinary derivative sheaf. By induction that ordinary derivative sheaf lies in the ordinary derivative sheaf of the preceding ordinary iterate, using monotonicity. This is the desired bound.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_mono: The zero-th iterate is the identity and preserves inclusions. At each successor the logarithmic operation preserves the inclusion between the preceding iterates, so induction proves monotonicity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_one: The first iterate applies the operation to the zero-th iterate, which is I.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_succ: The recursive definition applies the logarithmic derivative ideal sheaf operation once more at a successor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_zero: The zero-th iterate is the original ideal sheaf by definition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheaf_ideal: On an affine open, the logarithmic derivative ideal sheaf is defined by applying the ring-level operation to the two section ideals, using the base algebra structure on the section ring.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheaf_le_derivIdealSheaf: On each affine open the tangent derivations used for the logarithmic ideal are among all the derivations used for the ordinary derivative ideal. The latter contains the original ideal and all of the logarithmic generators, giving the inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheaf_mono: An inclusion of inputs gives an inclusion on every affine open. With P fixed, the ring-level logarithmic operation preserves each of those inclusions. This gives the inclusion of ideal sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdeal_basicOpen: The section ring of the basic open is the localization at f, with the same action of the base ring after restriction. The section ideals of P and I on the basic open are extensions of their ideals on U. The section ring on U is Noetherian, so the ideal of P is finitely generated, and its module of differentials is finitely presented. The localization formula for logarithmic derivative ideals now identifies the extended ideal with the ideal assigned to the basic open.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.app_comp_sectionsAlgebraMap: The scalar map is obtained by pulling back global sections of the base. Pulling these sections back through the morphism after restricting along p is pullback along the composite structural map. The equality follows from composition of section maps.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.app_sectionsAlgebraMap: Apply the compatibility of scalar structure maps with pullback to a.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_le_of_map_ideal_le: Let U be affine in X. The inverse image under the affine map is affine, and the ideal of D there is the kernel of restriction to its closed subscheme. By hypothesis the image of each element of the ideal of L on U belongs to this kernel. Its pullback under the composite immersion of that closed subscheme into X is zero. This gives containment of L in the kernel ideal sheaf of the composite. By the adjunction for extension and inverse image of ideal sheaves, the pullback of L lies in D.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_logDerivIdealSheafIterate_ker_le_d: Apply the closed-immersion comparison of the pulled-back logarithmic iterate with the ordinary iterate of the pulled-back ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comp_app_apply: Pullback of sections under a composite is the successive pullback along its two maps. Evaluating at a gives the formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_mono_of_le: At zero the inclusion is the original one. At a successor apply monotonicity of the derivative ideal operation to the inclusion for the preceding step.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_comap_le_deriv: For every affine open the ring-level comparison gives the containment of the extended section ideal in the corresponding section ideal of the target sheaf. The affine-morphism criterion for pullback containment then gives the sheaf inequality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdealSheafIterate_ideal_le: The pullback on sections of the affine open is a surjective k-algebra map because the morphism is a closed immersion and scalar maps commute with pullback. Its kernel is the section ideal of the kernel sheaf. Use the ring-level inequality for images of iterated logarithmic derivative ideals along this quotient. The extension of the original section ideal is contained in the section ideal of the pulled-back sheaf. Monotonicity of ordinary iteration therefore bounds the resulting ideal by the stated iterate on the inverse-image open.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.appLE_sectionsAlgebraMap: Pulling a base scalar section to U and then to V is the same as pulling it back along the composite structural map to V. This follows from composition of the section maps.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.bijective_appLE_image_of_isOpenImmersion: The open immersion identifies V with its open image. The resulting map of section rings is an isomorphism and is therefore bijective.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.bijective_hom_of_iso: An isomorphism of rings has an inverse ring homomorphism. The underlying functions are inverse, so the forward function is bijective.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_comap_eq_map_appLE: An open immersion identifies an affine source open with its image. On their section rings the map in the statement is the induced isomorphism. The pulled-back section ideal is the inverse image along the inverse ring isomorphism, which equals extension along the forward one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_comap_ideal_of: Take the image affine open of V. The section map from the image to V is an isomorphism, and the ideals of the pulled-back sheaves are extensions along this map. Both sheaf iterates on these opens are the corresponding ring iterates. Transport the ambient ring iterate along the section isomorphism, which sends it to the iterate for the extended boundary and input ideals.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_comap_of_isOpe: The two ideal sheaves have the same ideals on every affine open by the section comparison for the open immersion. This determines equality of the sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_appLE_logDerivIdealIterate_of_biject: The section ring on the source side of the ring map is Noetherian and its differential module is finitely presented. In particular P is finitely generated. The section map respects scalars by composition of structural maps. Apply the transport formula for a bijective ring map with these hypotheses.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_eq_comap_of_inverse: Every image of an element of J is sent back into J by the inverse, so the extended ideal is contained in the inverse image under the inverse map. Conversely an element of that inverse image is the forward image of its own inverse, which lies in J. This proves equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdealIterate_of_bijective: The bijective ring map is a localization away from one. The scalar compatibility makes it a localization of the given base algebra. Use the localization formula for iterated logarithmic derivative ideals.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_mem_pow_sub_one: Induct on n. At zero the derivative lands in the unit ideal. In the successor step write the higher power as the product of the preceding power and J. For a product ab from these two factors, the term a times the derivative of b lies in the preceding power. The other term lies in J times the power given by induction for the derivative of a, which is contained in the same preceding power. Additivity handles sums of such products.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_natCast_mul: Multiplication by the image of a natural number is repeated addition. Since a derivation is additive, it commutes with this multiplication.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.fin_cons_self_tail: At the first position the reconstructed tuple agrees with β by its choice of head. At each later position it agrees by the definition of the tail. Hence the functions agree at every index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.foldr_comm_of_comm: The result for an empty composition is immediate. In a nonempty composition commute E past the first map by hypothesis, then commute it past the composition of the tail by induction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.foldr_eq_of_eq_id_of_ne: All factors except the distinguished one are identities. This follows recursively by removing the first factor. If it is the distinguished factor, the tail is an identity composition. If it is an identity, the tail contains the distinguished factor and gives the desired map by induction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.foldr_eq_self_of_forall_eq_self: The empty composition fixes x. In a nonempty list the composition of the tail fixes x by induction, and the first map fixes that value by hypothesis.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.foldr_iterate_mem_pow_sub: Induct on the ordered family of derivations. The empty family makes no change. In a nonempty family the tail reduces the exponent by the sum of its iteration counts. Applying the first derivation its prescribed number of times reduces the exponent by that additional count. Truncated subtraction in succession is subtraction of their sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iterate_derivation_mem_pow_sub: With zero iterations the original containment is unchanged. Each application lowers the available ideal-power exponent by one, with truncation at zero. Apply the one-derivative estimate and the induction hypothesis to get the exponent n minus the total number of applications.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iterate_derivation_mul: At order zero the product is unchanged. Differentiate the formula at order n. The derivative commutes with the finite sum and the natural coefficients, and the Leibniz rule adds one application to either factor in each term. Reindex and combine the two sums by Pascal’s identity, obtaining the coefficients for order n + 1.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iterate_derivation_natCast_mul: The identity map commutes with multiplication by the natural scalar. The single-derivation compatibility is preserved by composing with another application, so induction gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iterate_derivation_sum: The identity preserves the finite sum. Each further derivative is additive and commutes with the sum, proving the identity by induction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_pow_sub_one_le: At n equal to zero the right side is the unit ideal. For positive n, the product of J with its preceding power is exactly the n-th power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_add: Apply composition of mixed derivatives for a family of pairwise commuting derivations.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_add_of_comm_forall: Induct on the size of the family. In the nonempty case split off the first derivation and apply induction to the tail. The first derivation commutes with each tail derivation and hence with every iterate and their ordered composite. Its powers can therefore move past the tail factors. Group its applications into the two prescribed counts, using the addition rule for powers of a single map. The resulting two successive mixed derivatives have indices β and α in that order.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_add_unitMultiIndex_apply: The addition rule for commuting derivations splits the mixed derivative into the unit-index derivative followed by the derivative with index α. The unit-index derivative is the single application at i.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_fun_zero: The function constantly zero is the zero multi-index. Apply the identity for that index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_mem_pow_sub: The mixed derivative is the ordered composition of the iterated derivatives. The power estimate for that composition subtracts the sum of all entries of the multi-index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_mul: Induct on the number of derivations in the family. With no derivations the only split is empty and the product stays unchanged. For a nonempty family, expand the tail derivative of the product by induction. Apply the prescribed iterate of the first derivation to each term, taking the natural coefficient outside and using the one-variable Leibniz formula on the two factors. Combining the split of the first count with each tail split gives all allowed multi-indices. The coefficient is the product of their coordinate binomial coefficients. The order of application in both factors is the same as in the original mixed derivative.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_mul_sub_sum_mem: The mixed Leibniz formula expands the product derivative over all splits of α. Remove those splits whose first part has total order r. In every remaining term, either the first part has order less than r or the second part has order less than s, since their orders add to r + s. The corresponding derivative then lies in a positive power of J by the order estimate. Thus each remaining product, and hence their sum, lies in J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_of_isEmpty: There are no derivations to apply. The empty composition is the identity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_succ: By definition the composition for a nonempty index first acts with the tail of the family and then applies the first derivation the specified number of times.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_unitMultiIndex: A unit multi-index prescribes one application at i and zero elsewhere. The ordered composition is therefore the derivation at i.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_zero: Every entry of the zero multi-index prescribes zero applications of its derivation. Each factor in the composition is the identity, so the composite fixes f.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_choose_succ_mul_eq: Separate the last term in the first sum and the first term in the second. The remaining terms have the same products after shifting the index by one. Their coefficients add by Pascal’s identity, giving the interior binomial coefficients for n + 1. Each boundary term already has coefficient one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_piFinset_succ: A tuple of allowed values consists uniquely of an allowed first value and a tuple of allowed tail values. Reindex the sum by this bijection and then sum over the first value and the tail in succession.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_unitMultiIndex: All entries except the designated one are zero, and the remaining entry is one. Thus the sum is one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.unitMultiIndex_apply: The unit multi-index is defined to have value one at its designated index and zero elsewhere.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coeff_eq: The coefficient is defined as the image of the iterated derivative multiplied by the image of the inverse factorial.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.factorial_inv_mul_choose: Start with the binomial identity that the coefficient times the two factorials of the split sizes equals the factorial of j. The factorials are nonzero in the rationals, so dividing by their product and by the factorial of j gives the equation there. Apply the algebra map to the target ring.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iterate_deriv_mul: In the repeated-addition formula, an integer count acting on a ring element is multiplication by its image in the ring. Replace each repeated-addition coefficient by that scalar factor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iterate_deriv_mul_eq_sum_nsmul: Induct on the number of applications. The formula at zero has only the original product. At each successor, apply additivity and the Leibniz rule to every term. Each term produces one term with an extra derivative on the first factor and one with an extra derivative on the second. In the interior, Pascal’s identity combines the two neighboring coefficients. The two endpoint products have coefficient one. This proves the iterated product rule with coefficients acting by repeated addition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mk_truncatedSeries_add: The truncated series preserves addition. The quotient map also preserves addition, giving the displayed equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mk_truncatedSeries_mul: The difference between the truncated series of the product and the product of the two series lies in J. Their classes are therefore equal, and the quotient map carries a product to the product of its classes.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mk_truncatedSeries_one: The truncated series of one is one for positive N, and its class in the quotient is one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mk_truncatedSeries_zero: The truncated series of zero is zero, and its class in the quotient is zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_Ico_mul_pow_eq_sum_range: Set j = i + k. The interval from i up to, but excluding, N corresponds to 0 ≤ k < N − i, and j − i becomes k. This changes the summand to exactly the one on the right.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_convolution_sub_mul_mem: Expand the product of the two truncated sums into terms indexed by pairs i,k each below N. The convolution sum uses precisely the pairs with i + k < N, by setting the total degree to i + k. Their difference is the negative of the terms with i + k at least N. Each of those terms contains β to a power at least N and hence is a multiple of β to the N-th power. They all lie in J, as does their signed sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_range_sum_range_succ_eq_sum_sum_Ico: Both sums run over pairs with 0 ≤ i ≤ j < N. The first groups by the larger index j, and the second groups by the smaller index i. Equivalently, increasing N adds the same terms with j equal to the old bound on both sides.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeriesRingHom_apply: The ring homomorphism is defined by evaluating the truncated series and taking its class modulo J. This gives its value at f.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_add: Every iterate of the additive derivation preserves addition. Apply this to every coefficient and use additivity of σ, then distribute the scalar factors and split the finite sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_apply: By definition the truncated series is the sum over degrees below N, with coefficient the image of the iterated derivative divided by its factorial, multiplied by the corresponding power of β.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_mul: At each degree j expand the derivative of the product by the iterated Leibniz rule. The ring map transports this sum and its products to S. For each split i and j − i, the binomial coefficient divided by j factorial becomes the product of the inverses of the two split factorials. Thus the coefficient of β to the j-th power is the sum of products of the two individual Taylor coefficients.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_mul_sub_mem: Use the convolution formula for the Taylor series of the product and express each individual Taylor series as the sum of its coefficients times powers of β. The difference is the convolution error, which belongs to J because β to the N-th power does.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_of_deriv_eq_zero: All positive iterates of D on f vanish because the first is zero and D fixes zero. Since N is positive, the sum contains the constant term. This is the only term left, and it equals σ(f).
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_one: Every derivation kills one. The series of an element killed by the derivation equals its constant term when N is positive, and σ sends one to one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_sub_mem_span_singleton: Subtracting σ(f) removes the degree-zero term since N is positive. Every remaining term has a positive power of β, hence has β as a factor. Their sum lies in the principal ideal generated by β.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_zero: Every iterate of D sends zero to zero, including the identity iterate. Each term is consequently zero after applying σ, so the sum vanishes.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_adapted_parameters: Choose generators of the maximal ideal of A with independent residue differentials. Clear denominators to replace them by images of elements of q. Each parameter is thereby multiplied by a unit, which preserves the generated ideal and scales its residue differential by a nonzero scalar because the parameter vanishes at the closed point. The original coordinate differentials give a basis over A by formal étaleness and localization. Complete the independent residue differentials of the parameters to a basis with a subset of the original coordinate differentials. Index the parameters by the complement of that subset, which has the same cardinality. The resulting tuple uses the chosen elements of q on the complement and the original coordinates elsewhere. Its differential determinant has nonzero residue in A since the reduced tuple is a basis. Compatibility of the coordinate determinant with localization then shows that the determinant g in S lies outside q. In the principal localization at g the determinant is a unit, while the selected parameters already generate the maximal ideal in A.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_fun_sum_smul_eq_of_mem_span: The sums indexed by the family form a submodule. Zero uses all zero coefficients, addition adds the coefficient functions, and scalar multiplication scales them. A coefficient function supported at one index with value one gives the corresponding generator. This submodule therefore contains the span and in particular contains x.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_local_parameters: Choose finite generators of the maximal ideal and select among them a family whose residue differentials form a basis of the span of all their residue differentials. The Leibniz rule shows that this span contains the residue differential of every element of the maximal ideal. Express such a differential in the selected basis and lift its coefficients to the local ring. Subtracting the resulting combination of the selected generators leaves an element with zero residue differential, so it lies in the square of the maximal ideal. The selected elements thus generate the maximal ideal modulo its square, and Nakayama’s lemma makes them generators of the ideal itself. Their residue differentials are independent by construction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_section_mod_maximalIdeal_sq: Write m for the maximal ideal and κ for the residue field. The surjection A/m² → κ has square-zero kernel m/m². Formal smoothness of κ over k lifts its identity map to a k-algebra section. For each a in A, choose a representative w(a) of the section applied to the residue of a. Then a and w(a) have the same residue. The section preserves addition, scalar multiplication, and multiplication, and these identities for w hold modulo m². If a lies in m, its residue is zero, so w(a) represents zero in A/m².
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_maximalIdeal_sq_of_tmul_D_eq_zero: Use the section of A/m² → κ and subtract its composite with the residue map from the quotient map A → A/m². The difference takes values in m/m². It is a k-derivation because the differences multiply to zero, and it takes each element of m to its own class in m/m². Since m annihilates the target, the linear map induced by this derivation on the differential module factors through the residue tensor product. The hypothesis says the differential of x is zero in that tensor product. Its class under the induced map is therefore zero in m/m², so x lies in m².
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.residue_det_ne_zero_of_basis_tmul: Reduce the original module basis to the residue field. In that basis, the coordinate matrix of the given reduced vectors is the entrywise reduction of the original coordinate matrix. Taking determinants commutes with this reduction. The given reduced vectors form a basis, so their determinant is nonzero in the residue field.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coordVectorInl_inl: The first coordinate vector is formed by retaining the pullback coordinates on the first index block and putting zero on the second. A first-block index selects the original pullback section.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coordVectorInl_inr: At a second-block index, the first coordinate vector takes the prescribed zero value.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coordVectorInr_inl: The second coordinate vector has zero in every first-block position, so it is zero at the given index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coordVectorInr_inr: On the second index block, the second coordinate vector retains the pullback sections. Its value at b is the pullback of the b-th coordinate along f.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackCoord_def: The coordinate section associated to f is defined by pulling the indicated affine-space coordinate back to a global section on Y.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.affineOpenIsoSpec_hom_appTop_apply: The affine identification uses first the spectrum of the global sections of the open subscheme and then the isomorphism of that ring with the section ring on W′. Naturality for spectrum maps transfers a through the inverse section-ring identification. The affine comparison then pulls that section back unchanged to the open subscheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.affineSpaceOpenIsoSpecMvPolynomial_hom_a: The constant polynomial a is the pullback of the base section a under the spectrum map of the coefficient inclusion. That map corresponds to the projection from relative affine space to its base. Transport to W′ using the affine identification. Compatibility of the projection with this transport gives the pullback of the section on the open subscheme corresponding to a.

Over the spectrum of the section ring on W′, the identification of affine space with the spectrum of a polynomial ring sends the variable section to the corresponding affine coordinate. Pulling back along the affine-space map induced by the identification of W′ with that spectrum preserves each coordinate. This gives the claimed coordinate on affine space over W′.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.algebraEtale_comp_equiv: Transport the target of the étale algebra map along the target isomorphism. The transported algebra remains étale over R. The source isomorphism is itself étale, so composing with it gives an étale algebra over R′.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.algebraEtale_congr: The two ring maps coincide, so they induce the same algebra structure. The étaleness condition on that structure transfers directly.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.algebraEtale_of_ringHomEtale: An étale ring map is one whose associated algebra structure is étale. The hypothesis gives precisely that property for the algebra induced by f.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.chartAlgebra_etale:
Identify the relative affine space over W with the spectrum of the polynomial ring over the sections on W. The chart map followed by this isomorphism is étale between affine schemes, so its map on global sections is étale. Transport this map to the polynomial ring and the ring of sections on V by their canonical isomorphisms.

To identify the transported map with chart evaluation, compare the polynomial generators. A constant is pulled back along the projection to W and then along the chart, which is the coefficient map. A variable is pulled back as the corresponding affine coordinate section, which is the variable value in evaluation. Both maps therefore agree on all polynomials, proving étaleness of the chart algebra.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.chartAlgebra_formallyEtale: The chart algebra is étale by the preceding result, and every étale algebra is formally étale.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.chartAlgebra_isScalarTower: The polynomial algebra on V is induced by evaluation. A section on W enters the polynomial ring as a constant. Evaluating it yields its pullback along h by the constant formula, which is the direct action of the base section ring on V. The agreement gives the scalar tower.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.chartEvalHom_C: Evaluate the equality between the coefficient map of polynomial evaluation and the section pullback at the scalar section a.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.chartEvalHom_comp_C: The polynomial evaluation acts on constants by the coefficient map. That coefficient map pulls sections back along the chart followed by the projection. The hypothesis identifies that composite with the restriction of h, and the section-ring identifications therefore make it the section pullback along h. Thus the two ring maps agree on every coefficient.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comp_appTop_apply: The operation of pulling back global sections is contravariant. Pullback along the composite first pulls back z along the second map and then along the first.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isoSpec_hom_appTop_apply: The canonical map from the affine scheme Z to the spectrum of its global section ring induces the canonical identification of global sections with that ring. A section corresponding to a on the spectrum therefore pulls back to a on Z.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.resLE_appTop_conj_topIso_eq_appLE: Substitute the formula for the pullback on global sections of the open subschemes. On each end the identification and its inverse cancel, leaving the section pullback from W′ to V′.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.resLE_appTop_eq: Identify global sections of each open subscheme with sections over the corresponding open of the ambient scheme. Under these identifications, pulling back global sections along the restricted map is the section pullback from W′ to V′. This gives the stated composite.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.specMap_appTop_apply: Under the canonical identifications of a ring with the global sections of its spectrum, pulling back along the spectrum map of u is the ring map u. Applying this identification to a gives the displayed section.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.algebraMap_eq_coordRingHom: The chart algebra structure is the one induced by the coordinate-ring map, so its structure map is that ring map.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.algebra_etale: The structure map of the chart algebra is the étale coordinate-ring map. This is precisely étaleness of the algebra.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.algebra_formallyEtale: By the preceding result the chart algebra is étale. Formal étaleness is one of the conditions of étaleness.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.coordRingHom_C: Evaluate the formula for the composite with the constant inclusion at a. The result is its scalar section on U.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.coordRingHom_X: The global section of affine space corresponding to the j-th polynomial variable is the j-th affine coordinate. The chart ring map pulls this section back to U, which is the definition of the j-th chart coordinate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.coordRingHom_comp_C: On the polynomial spectrum the inclusion of constants corresponds to the projection to the spectrum of k. Transport that projection through the affine-space identification. By the defining commutative square of the chart, its composite with the chart is the structure map of the open subscheme U. Pullback on global sections and the identification with sections over U therefore give the scalar map induced by p.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.coordRingHom_def: The coordinate-ring map is defined by identifying polynomials with global sections of affine space, pulling those sections back along the chart, and identifying the resulting global sections with sections over U.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.coordRingHom_etale: Both the affine chart domain and the affine space over k are affine. Hence the étale chart induces an étale map on their global section rings. The coordinate-ring map is this map transported through the canonical identifications of the two rings. Because those identifications are isomorphisms, the coordinate-ring map is étale.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.coord_def: The chart coordinate is defined by pulling the affine coordinate back to a global section of the chart domain, then identifying it with a section over U in X.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.etaleCoordinates_coord: In the chart algebra, the coordinate is the image of its polynomial variable under the coordinate-ring map. The variable formula identifies that image with the geometric chart coordinate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.ideal_eq_span_coord:
On the affine scheme U, the global ideal of the restricted ideal sheaf is the extension of the original section ideal on U along the canonical section-ring isomorphism. The global ideal of the chart ideal is generated by the affine coordinate sections indexed by S pulled back along the chart. Under the same section-ring isomorphism these generators correspond to the chart coordinates viewed as sections over U.

The restriction hypothesis identifies the two global ideals on the open subscheme. Extend back along the inverse section-ring isomorphism. The original section ideal is therefore generated by the chart coordinates indexed by S.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.EtaleChart.isScalarTower: The scalar action through the polynomial ring sends a scalar to a constant polynomial and then applies the chart ring map. The constant formula identifies its value with the direct scalar section given by p. Agreement of the two scalar maps gives the tower.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.affineSpaceGlobalSectionsHom_X: Under pullback from affine space to the polynomial spectrum, the j-th coordinate becomes the section of the j-th variable. The map from polynomials to sections on affine space applies the inverse of that pullback. It therefore sends the variable back to the coordinate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.affineSpace_specIso_hom_comp_specMap_C: The canonical identification of affine space with the polynomial spectrum is over the spectrum of K. The projection of the polynomial spectrum is induced by the inclusion of constants, so composing the identification with that projection gives the affine-space structure map.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.affineSpace_specIso_inv_appTop_coord: The standard isomorphism from the spectrum of the coordinate polynomial ring to affine space pulls the j-th affine coordinate back to the global section corresponding to the j-th polynomial variable.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.appLE_top_comp_topIso_inv: Use the preceding description of the direct section pullback as global pullback followed by the section-ring identification on V. Composing with the inverse identification cancels it and leaves the global pullback.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.appTop_comp_topIso_hom: Pullback of a global section along the inclusion of V followed by f is pullback by f followed by restriction to V. Identifying the result on the open subscheme V with a section on V gives the direct section map. The two restriction composites agree by functoriality of the presheaf.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.appTop_hom_appTop_inv_apply: The pullbacks on global sections induced by an isomorphism and its inverse are inverse ring maps, since pullback takes the composite identity to the identity. Applying the two pullbacks in succession returns x.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comp_presheafMap_comp_presheafMap: Compose the two restriction maps by functoriality of the presheaf. They are induced by the composite arrow, which equals the direct arrow because the category of opens has at most one arrow between any two objects. Precomposing with h gives the asserted equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_map_topIso_inv_injective: Apply ideal extension along the inverse isomorphism to both equal ideals in the global section ring of V. Each double extension is extension by the identity and therefore returns its original ideal. This gives equality of the original ideals.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ι_appLE_top_eq_topIso_inv: The section map of the inclusion identifies a section over V with the same section viewed globally on the open subscheme V. This is the inverse of the identification in the other direction.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPrime_span_singleton_algebraMap_etaleC: The localization A is regular local by the étale localization theorem. The chosen coordinate lies in q, so its localized image lies in the maximal ideal of A. For this singleton set of coordinates, the étale cotangent-space result says that the class of the image is linearly independent in the cotangent space. The regular local ring criterion for an element with independent cotangent class gives that the ideal generated by the localized coordinate is prime.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.algebraMap_coordPolynomialRing_injective: The coordinate polynomial ring is a domain and the étale target is flat over it. A nonzero element of this domain acts injectively on the target by flatness.
