Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.F_perm: Permuting the triples permutes the list of their matrix terms. Its sum is unchanged by commutativity of matrix addition, so taking the determinant of the identity minus that sum gives the same polynomial.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.S1_mem_OmF: The carrier of S1 requires each multivariate coefficient function to lie in the subalgebra of functions from T. Unfolding that carrier replaces each such membership by the assertion that the coefficient function comes from T, which is the right-hand side.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.X_mem_polyS: The coefficient of X in degree one is 1, and all its other coefficients are zero. The subring S contains both values.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.alg_identity: Let P = 1+x+⋯+xᴺ and Y be the sum of the list ys. For each power of x, distribute left multiplication over the sum Y. The total sum inside the second factor is then PY. The finite geometric identity and x^(N+1) = 0 give (1−x)P = 1. Hence (1−x)(1−PY) = (1−x)−Y = 1−(x+Y). The products keep x and its powers on the left throughout.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.allD: Induct on the amount j by which the lower degree bound can be raised before it reaches N+1. If j = 0, all terms vanish in the truncation and the determinant equals 1. For the successor step, increasing the minimum degree from D to D+1 makes the induction hypothesis available. The degree-elimination lemma transfers that result back to lists of minimum degree D.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.base: In the quotient modulo X^(N+1), every scalar monomial in the list is zero because its degree is at least N+1. Thus the sum of matrix terms vanishes. The image of F is the determinant of the identity, which is 1.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.charpolyRev_map: Apply the coefficient ring homomorphism to the determinant that defines the reversed characteristic polynomial. It commutes with determinants, fixes the polynomial variable, and maps the constant matrix entries through f. Entry by entry the result is the defining matrix for the reversed characteristic polynomial of M with entries mapped through f.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.charpoly_comp: The reversed characteristic polynomial of ρ(g) is the determinant of I−Xρ(g), with the matrix entries regarded as constants. Substitute C(c)Xᵈ for X in this determinant for L = (c,d,g). Substitution fixes scalar entries and commutes with determinants. The resulting matrix is I minus the term attached to L.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.comp_mem_polyS: Expand p(q) as the finite sum of C(pₑ)qᵉ over the degrees in p. Each constant C(pₑ) belongs to the coefficient subring, and every power of q does too. Closure under products and finite sums gives the result.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.core: Truncate at degree k. The degree-elimination result with initial degree bound 1 puts the class of F in the image of the polynomials over S. Choose a polynomial q over S representing that class. The difference F−q is divisible by X^(k+1), so its coefficient in degree k is zero. Thus the degree-k coefficient of F is the corresponding coefficient of q and belongs to S.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.det_eq_coeff: In a subsingleton ring the two values agree. Otherwise let d be the matrix dimension. The characteristic polynomial has degree d, so reversing it makes its constant coefficient the degree-d coefficient of the reversed polynomial. The constant coefficient of the characteristic polynomial is (−1)ᵈ det M. Multiplication by (−1)ᵈ gives the asserted formula because its square is 1.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.det_poly_statement:
For each matrix aᵢ choose its finite representation as a sum of group matrices with coefficient functions from T. Multiply each coefficient function by the multivariate variable Xᵢ. The resulting polynomial-valued function belongs to S1 because its only possibly nonzero coefficient is the original function. Lift the group matrices to matrices of constant multivariate polynomials, retaining their dependence on the test point. Evaluation at a point commutes with the reversed characteristic polynomial, so its only possibly nonzero multivariate coefficient comes from the original characteristic coefficient function. The input hypothesis puts that function in T.

Use these weighted group matrices as the letters of the determinant argument, all with degree one in the auxiliary polynomial variable. The core result puts the coefficient in degree d, the matrix dimension, into S1. Since the letters all have degree one, their determinant polynomial is the reversed characteristic polynomial of the summed weighted matrix. The sign formula converts that coefficient to the determinant, still in S1.

At each test point, expand the finite sum and use the chosen representations of the aᵢ. The weighted matrix evaluates to the sum of Xᵢaᵢ with entries mapped to constant multivariate polynomials. Evaluation commutes with the determinant. Taking the requested multivariate coefficient now gives a function from T by the defining condition of S1.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.geom_list: For N = 0 both sides equal 1−x. At the next step the finite sum acquires x^(N+1). Left multiplication by 1−x adds x^(N+1)−x^(N+2) to the previous value 1−x^(N+1). This gives the required value at N+1. The calculation uses only powers of the same element and works in a noncommutative ring.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.key:
Work in the coefficient ring modulo X^(N+1). Let x be the matrix term of L₀ there. The positive X-degree of L₀ makes x^(N+1) zero. For each term y from the rest of the list, the new triples represent the products xy through xᴺy by the formula for the new matrix terms. Thus the eliminated list sums to (1+x+⋯+xᴺ)Y, where Y is the original sum of the rest.

Apply the algebraic identity to factor I−(x+Y) as (I−x) times the identity minus the new sum. The quotient map commutes with determinants, and the determinant of a matrix product is the product of determinants over the commutative coefficient ring. This gives the asserted factorization in the quotient.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.letter_mem: By the substitution formula, the single-letter determinant is the reversed characteristic polynomial of ρ(g) evaluated at C(c)Xᵈ. The characteristic coefficients lie in S by hypothesis, and the substituted monomial has its coefficients in S because c belongs to S. Composition preserves this coefficient condition. Passing to the quotient gives membership in the image subring.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.mapMatrix_smul_zero: The entry in position (i,j) of the mapped matrix is the product of the images of a and Mᵢⱼ. The first factor is zero, so every entry vanishes.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.mem_mainNotions_iff_fromT: The carrier of the subalgebra is defined to consist of the functions from T. Membership therefore says exactly that the function comes from T.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.piN_eq_zero: Since d ≥ N+1, the monomial C(c)Xᵈ is divisible by X^(N+1). It therefore vanishes in the quotient by that principal ideal.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.stepD:
Induct on the number of letters of degree exactly D. With no such letters, all degrees are at least D+1 and the given higher-degree result applies. Otherwise move one degree-D letter to the front and factor it out by the determinant factorization. Its single-letter factor belongs to the image subring by the single-letter coefficient result.

In the remaining list, the old letters retain their coefficients and degrees. Each new letter multiplies an old coefficient by a positive power of the removed one, so the coefficient remains in S. Its degree is the old degree plus a positive multiple of D and is strictly larger than D. Thus the number of degree-D letters drops by exactly one, and the induction hypothesis puts the remaining determinant in the image subring. Multiply the two factors there.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sum_flat: Induct on the outer list. The empty list gives zero. For a head a followed by a tail, the flattened list is h(a) appended to the flattened tail. Its sum after applying f splits accordingly, and the induction hypothesis identifies the second sum.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.term_newL: Write L₀ = (c₀,d₀,g₀) and L = (c,d,g). The new triple has scalar c₀ᵏc, degree kd₀+d, and monoid element g₀ᵏg. Multiplicativity of the representation and of the constant-polynomial map gives the matrix factor ρ(g₀)ᵏρ(g), with entries mapped into R[X]. Multiplying the scalar monomials gives C(c₀ᵏc)X^(kd₀+d). This is the product of the kth power of the term for L₀ with the term for L, in that order.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.g_ideal_valuation_statement:
Let S₁ = [b−a+1,b]. The hypothesis b ≥ 2a+η+1 puts S₁ strictly above the low interval for S₂, and the other interval for S₂ starts at b+1. Thus the two sets are disjoint. The Lagrange ideal lifting theorem supplies ideal membership at exponent E, the supremum over j₀ in S₁ of the valuation sum on S₂ and on S₁ with j₀ removed. Its association hypothesis is exactly the one assumed for the differences of c.

For a fixed j₀, split the sum into S₁ with j₀ removed and the high and low portions of S₂. Their differences j₀−j lie in windows of lengths a, S+a, and 2η+a, respectively. All differences are nonzero by disjointness and the removal of j₀. The interval endpoints and b+S ≤ h give |j₀−j| ≤ h+η. Apply the window valuation estimate to each of the three parts. The lengths add to 3a+S+2η, and each logarithm is at most lam(ℓ,h+η). This bounds every value in the supremum and hence E. If S₁ is empty, E is zero and the bound follows by nonnegativity.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.winDiff: Reindex by the injective map j ↦ j₀−j. The image lies in the half-open window starting at lo with length L. Zero is absent because j₀ is absent from T, and the absolute values are bounded by D. Apply the valuation window estimate to this image.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.g_coeff_valuation_statement:
Split S₂ at b. Combine its portion above b with the indices in [b−a+1,b] other than j₀, since these two sets are disjoint. The other portion of S₂ lies in [1−η,η+a]. Reindex both sums injectively by i = j₀−j. The first image lies in the half-open interval starting at j₀−b−S−a of length 2a+S. The second lies in the interval starting at j₀−η−a of length 2η+a. Neither contains zero, since j₀ was removed from the central interval and the two ranges for S₂ lie outside it. The bounds on b and S also give |i| ≤ 2(h+η) in both images.

Apply the valuation window estimate to both images and sum. The length contribution is (3a+S+2η)/(ℓ−1). The logarithmic contribution is twice log base ℓ of 2(h+η), which is at most 3 lam(ℓ,h+η) by the definition of lam and nonnegativity of that logarithm.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sum_shift_val: The map j ↦ j₀−j is injective, so replacing the indices by their images preserves the sum. The weight of each image index i is vℓ(i).

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.length_quotient_le_of_pow_smul:
Let A be the sum of FFs and ℓ^(e′)M. Multiplying the first summand by ℓ^e puts it in J by hypothesis, and the second summand already lies in J and remains there after scaling. Thus ℓ^e annihilates A/(A∩J). The submodule generator bound controls its length by the rank of M times e times the length of O/(ℓ).

Use the sequence A/(A∩J) → M/J → M/(A+J). The first map is injective, and the second is a surjection. Its kernel consists of classes represented by a sum a+j, hence by a alone. This proves exactness and gives length additivity. Finally M/(A+J) is a quotient of M/A and has at most its length. Combine the two bounds.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.disj: Choose the separating function u for S and let g be its action on V. By the definition of Vₓ, g acts on it by the image of u(x) in the fraction field. For x in S this eigenvalue is zero. For x outside S it is nonzero, since the field embedding is injective. Thus VS for S lies in the zero eigenspace, and VS for the complement lies in the sum of the nonzero eigenspaces. Independence of eigenspaces at distinct eigenvalues makes these two spaces disjoint.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.exists_sep: For each pair y ≠ x choose a function f in T with f(y) ≠ f(x). Subtract the constant function f(x). This factor vanishes at x and is nonzero at y. For fixed y, multiply these factors over all x ≠ y, using 1 at x = y. The result eᵧ lies in T and has support exactly {y}, since O is a domain. Sum the eᵧ over y outside S. At any point of S all terms vanish, and at a point outside S exactly its own term survives.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.q_numerical_identity:
Put d = ℓ−1 > 0. The natural-number quotient H′ / (ℓ−1) is at most H′/d in the reals. Combine it with the rational term in the bound on eW to get H′/d + H′ℓ/d² = H′(2ℓ−1)/d². This is at most H(2ℓ−1)/d² because H′ ≤ H.

If H is positive, H′+1 ≤ 2H, so log base ℓ of H′+1 is at most log base ℓ of 2H. If H = 0, then H′ = 0 and the logarithmic bound with the added 1 holds under Lean’s real logarithm convention. Substitute these bounds, cancel the +1 and −1 from the left side, and use the definition of aR.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.ramified_valuation_inequality:
Write ℓ as a unit times ϖ^e, where e > 0. Thus ℓ is a nonunit. For each i between 0 and y, write the binomial coefficient choosing i from y as ℓ^vᵢ times a positive integer prime to ℓ. The latter is a unit in O. Indeed, its Bézout relation with ℓ expresses 1 as a sum of two terms, and the term divisible by ℓ is a nonunit. In the local ring the other term must be a unit.

Expand p₁^y by the binomial theorem. Its ith summand is a unit series times X^(ℓi) times the constant series ϖ^(e(vᵢ+y−i)). The series is a unit because it is a product of the prime-to-ℓ factor, powers of the given units, and a power of the unit relating ℓ to ϖ^e. The X-exponents are distinct. The ideal-membership criterion for such a sum says that each term either has X-exponent at least b or has ϖ-exponent at least t.

Set i₀ = floor((b−1)/ℓ). Then ℓi₀ < b ≤ ℓ(i₀+1) and b ≤ ℓy, so i₀ < y. The criterion gives t/e ≤ vᵢ₀+y−i₀. The binomial coefficient valuation is at most the integer logarithm of y to base ℓ, which in turn is at most the real logarithm. Also i₀ ≥ b/ℓ−1. Substituting gives the claimed bound with room to spare.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.geom_sum_range_mul_one_sub: Use induction on n. The empty sum yields zero on both sides. Increasing n by one adds x^n(1−x) to the product. Combining it with the inductive value 1−x^n gives 1−x^(n+1).
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.remainder_bound_of_tsum: Let d = ℓ−1, x = 1/d, L = log base ℓ of h, and C be the ceiling of 1+log base ℓ of 2h+1. Since h ≥ 1, we have 2h+1 ≤ 3h and log base ℓ of 3 ≤ 1. The ceiling bound gives C ≤ 3+L. Apply the two-level geometric estimate with initial coefficient 2G, tail coefficient 2h, and common offset C+3. This gives s ≤ (2G+2hx^j+C+3)/(1−x). Apply rr_arith with y = x^j and q = 1/(1−x) = d/(d−1). Its term hy/d equals h/d^(j+1), giving the desired remainder bound.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.rr_arith: Insert the bound on s and the value q = d/(d−1) into the estimate for r. This gives r ≤ (2G+2hy+C+3)F+C, where F = (d+1)/(d(d−1)). For d ≥ 2, clearing positive denominators shows F ≤ 10/(d+1), F ≤ 3/d, and F ≤ 3/2. For the 10/(d+1) and 3/2 bounds, the differences are 11+(d−2)(9d+6) and (d−2)(3d+1)/2, respectively. The 3/d bound reduces to d+1 ≤ 3(d−1). Apply these bounds to the G, hy, and C+3 terms, respectively. Then C ≤ 3+L bounds (C+3)·3/2+C by 12+5L/2 ≤ 20(L+1).
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.tsum_le_two_level: The nonnegative sequence is summable by its geometric majorant. Split the sum before index j. The first j terms contribute at most (A+D)(1−x^j)/(1−x). The tail contributes at most (B+D)x^j/(1−x), by shifting the index and summing the geometric series. Adding gives (A+Bx^j+D−Ax^j)/(1−x). Drop the nonnegative subtracted term Ax^j/(1−x).

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.iter_nzd: Induct on n. For n = 0 the hypothesis is already the desired membership. In the successor case write ℓ^(n+1)z as ℓ(ℓ^n z). The one-factor saturation condition gives ℓ^n z in the ideal, and the induction hypothesis gives z in the ideal.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.saturation_criterion: Identify A with its image in its fraction field. Choose b = f′x in A and a in A with fa = ℓ^k x. Multiplication by f′ gives ℓ^k b = f′fa in the fraction field and hence in A. Saturation of (f′), applied k times, gives b = f′c for some c in A. Cancel the nonzero f′ in the field to obtain x = c. Now ℓ^k c = fa in A. Apply saturation of (f) k times to obtain c = fd, as required.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.submodule_generator_count:
First bound the length of O/(ℓ^n) by n times the length of O/(ℓ). At n = 0 the quotient is zero. For the induction step the natural map O/(ℓ^(n+1)) → O/(ℓ^n) is onto. Its kernel is a quotient of O/(ℓ), via multiplication by ℓ^n, since each representative in the kernel is a multiple of ℓ^n. Length additivity gives the bound at n+1.

Now put Q = F∩P. Over the principal ideal domain, F has a finite basis of size k at most the rank of M. The classes of its basis elements generate F/Q, and the assumption says ℓ^e kills every class. Sending one standard generator to each basis class therefore gives a surjection from k copies of O/(ℓ^e) onto F/Q. Add the lengths of these copies, apply the bound at n = e, and replace k by the rank of M.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.len_base: Choose a basis of R of cardinality r. In coordinates, the image of −ℓ·id is exactly the vectors whose entries are multiples of ℓ. Each such vector has a preimage by choosing a multiplier for every coordinate and negating it. The quotient is therefore the product of r copies of O/(ℓ). Add their lengths.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.len_coker_add:
The commutative squares induce maps A/a(A) → B/b(B) → C/c(C). The second map is surjective because g is. If f(x) = b(y), then c(g(y)) = g(f(x)) = 0. Injectivity of c gives g(y) = 0, so y = f(z) by exactness. Then f(x) = f(a(z)), and injectivity of f gives x = a(z). This proves injectivity of the first induced map.

If a class represented by y lies in the kernel of the second map, write g(y) = c(u) and lift u to v in B. Then g(y−b(v)) = 0. Exactness writes y−b(v) as f(z), so the class of y comes from A/a(A). Conversely g f = 0 makes every image class vanish. Length additivity on the resulting short exact sequence gives the formula.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.len_main:
Induct on n. For n = 0, q = 0 and the formula for the zero operator applies. For the step, use the exact sequence ker q → R → im q, where the second map is q with its codomain restricted. The operator on the kernel is zero. The restriction to the image is killed by the preceding power, since every element of the image already has the form q(x). The three operators q−ℓ·id commute with the sequence, and the one on the image is injective by nilpotence and torsion-freeness.

Use additivity of cokernel length, then apply the induction hypothesis to the kernel and image, which are finite free submodules over the principal ideal domain. Their ranks add to the rank of R, by the quotient–image isomorphism and rank additivity. The two length formulas combine into the claimed one.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.length_pi_zero_bound: Choose an exponent n with q^n = 0. Then q^(n+1) is zero as well, so the nilpotent-operator length formula applies at n with the given scalar and yields the desired length formula.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sub_smul_one_injective: Take x in the kernel of q−ℓ·id. Then q(x) = ℓx, and linearity gives q^k(x) = ℓ^k x by induction. At k = n the nilpotence hypothesis gives ℓ^n x = 0. Since ℓ^n is nonzero and the module is torsion-free, x = 0.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.sigma_exponent_le_real: Write d = ℓ−1 and m = j−1. Use Mpar ≤ (h+2g)/d + 1, the floor bound on the integer quotient. In the argument of the ceiling, the contribution from 3g is at most 9g/4 because ℓ/d² ≤ 3/4. The remaining Mpar contribution is bounded by the sum of (h+2g)ℓ/(d³ℓ^m) and (ℓ/d²)/ℓ^m. For the first use ℓ ≤ 3d/2 and d^m ≤ ℓ^m. For the second use ℓ^m ≥ 1 and ℓ/d² ≤ 3/4. Finally allow the existing 1 and up to 1 more for the ceiling. This yields the stated constant 11/4.
Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.total_exponent_le_eight_hundred:
Put T = h/(ℓ−1)^(j+1), U = g·ell, and L = log base ℓ of h. Unfold the total exponent to obtain 4rr+8σ+4U+2kap. Since G/ℓ ≤ g/3, the rr bound is 20(g/3+T+L+1). Using (ℓ−1)^(j+1) ≥ 4 in the sigma estimate gives the sigma exponent σ ≤ 3T/2+3g+11/4. For kap, use 4g/(ℓ−1) ≤ 2g and log base ℓ of 2h ≤ L+1.

Substitution gives coefficients 92 for T and 90 for L. All remaining terms are bounded by 269U, using g ≤ U, ell ≤ U, and 1 ≤ U. Since T, U, and L are nonnegative, the resulting sum is at most 800(T+U+L).

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.truncation_signature_bound:
Put d = ℓ−1. For T ≥ 0, set A = ℓy−T. Multiplying the first general inequality by d reduces it to A ≤ d max(0,A), which holds because d ≥ 1. Thus ℓy/d − max(0,ℓy−T) ≤ T/d. Take T = X and T = η+M. Enlarging these right sides by the stipulated nonnegative amounts gives the first two bounds.

For the third bound set B = dy−X/ℓ. Multiplication by d² rewrites the left side as X + ℓB − d² max(0,B). If B ≤ 0, the correction is nonpositive. If B ≥ 0, it is (ℓ−d²)B, again nonpositive since ℓ ≥ 3. Divide by d² to get the stronger bound X/d², then add the allowed 1.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.pow_mem_span_pow_mul: Expand the yth power as u^y π₀^y q^((ℓ−1)y). Since M ≤ y and η ≤ (ℓ−1)y, factor π₀^M from the second factor and q^η from the third. The remaining factor is u^y π₀^(y−M) q^((ℓ−1)y−η). This exhibits membership in the ideal generated by π₀^M q^η.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.truncation_remainder_bound:
Put A = π₀+ℓ. If y = 0, the assumed inequality forces c = 0, so 1 is already a generator. For y ≥ 1, reserve one factor π₀ and expand the remaining factor π₀^(y−1) as (A−ℓ)^(y−1). The term indexed by m contains π₀ A^(m+(ℓ−1)y) and (−ℓ)^(y−1−m), multiplied by a binomial coefficient.

If y−1−m ≥ c, this term is divisible by ℓ^c. Otherwise m ≥ y−c, so m+(ℓ−1)y ≥ ℓy−c ≥ K by the assumed inequality. In this case it is divisible by π₀ A^K. Every term is in the two-generator ideal, and so is their sum.

Formalism/TruncatedSeriesCounting/Trunca.unit_coefficient_power_mod:
The definition of p₁ gives p₁ − uX^ℓ = C(ℓ)ε. Since a−b divides a^y−b^y, write p₁^y = (uX^ℓ)^y + C(ℓ)W for some series W. The coefficient of degree ℓy in (uX^ℓ)^y is the constant coefficient of u raised to y. Thus the coefficient of p₁^y has the required congruence modulo ℓ.

In the local-ring case, the constant coefficient of the unit u is a unit and remains one after taking the yth power. The correction term belongs to the maximal ideal because ℓ does. If the sum belonged to the maximal ideal, subtracting the correction would place that unit in the ideal, a contradiction. The coefficient is therefore a unit.

Main.lean.LFunction_eq_zero_re: Fix a character and a zero in the open critical strip. The critical-strip conclusion of the combined nonvanishing theorem applies to all characters and forces real part 1/2.
Main.lean.LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive: Apply the critical-line theorem for primitive characters to the given zero in the open critical strip. It gives Re(s) = 1/2.
Main.lean.LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re: Fix a Dirichlet character and a point strictly to the right of the critical line. The assumption on the character or the point excludes the exceptional pair of the principal character and s = 1, so the right half-plane nonvanishing theorem applies.
Main.lean.riemannHypothesis: Apply the reduction from right half-plane nonvanishing for Dirichlet L-functions to the Riemann Hypothesis. The nonvanishing theorem for every character supplies its hypothesis.
Main.lean.riemannZeta_eq_zero_re: Let s be a zero of the zeta function distinct from 1 and from the negative even integers. The Riemann Hypothesis established above applies to precisely these zeros and gives real part 1/2.

Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.allChi: Apply the right half-plane nonvanishing theorem for every Dirichlet character to the given character and point.
Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.claimAll: Start with right half-plane nonvanishing for every character. The Dirichlet critical-strip reduction and the zeta-zero reduction give the other two conclusions from this same input. Combine the three claims.
Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.critAll: Fix a primitive character χ and a zero s with 0 < Re(s) < 1. Apply the primitive-character critical-line criterion with the right half-plane nonvanishing theorem. The criterion gives Re(s) = 1/2.
Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.rhOfAll: The reduction to the Riemann Hypothesis requires right half-plane nonvanishing for all characters. Apply it using the preceding nonvanishing theorem.
